docs.title: Data Assimilation for Lake Hydrodynamic Models
docs.text: Integrating observations into operational lake models to improve forecast accuracy for the Alplakes platform.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This repository implements a data assimilation (DA) framework for lake hydrodynamic models operated as part of the Alplakes project at Eawag. The framework blends high-resolution in situ measurements and satellite remote sensing data into 1D and 3D hydrodynamic simulations, correcting model states in near-real time to produce more accurate lake forecasts across the European Alpine region.

Alplakes provides operational hydrodynamic simulations for over 200 lakes, combining 1D (Simstrat) and 3D (Delft3D-FLOW, MITgcm) models with remote sensing products. Data assimilation is the mechanism that bridges the gap between model predictions and observed reality, reducing forecast errors and quantifying uncertainty.

docs.title: Run configuration
docs.text:
One run is described by one flat dict: as a JSON file for the command line, or passed directly by a host program.

python src/assimilate.py run examples/enkf.json            # from a file
python src/assimilate.py run --sim-dir inputs/upperlugano --obs obs.csv --perturbations p.json \
    --start 2025-01-01 --end 2025-12-31 --out run/upperlugano      # from flags

import assimilator
result = assimilator.run(cfg)          # cfg: the same keys as the JSON

assimilator.config.build_config fills the defaults below, makes every path absolute, derives the engine's file names and validates the result before anything runs. Relative paths resolve against the current working directory, never against this repository. Keys starting with _ are comments and are dropped. A "lakes" map (the former per-lake blocks) is rejected: one config is one run.

{
    "lake": "upperlugano",
    "algorithm": "EnKF",
    "n_members": 20,
    "start_date": "2025-01-01",
    "end_date": "2025-12-31",
    "model_inputs_path": "inputs/upperlugano",
    "ensemble_base": "run/upperlugano",
    "obs_file": "observations/upperlugano/temperature_filtered_h06_1d.csv",
    "sigma_obs": {"mixed": 0.299, "stratified": 0.586},
    "perturbations_file": "upperlugano.json"
}

docs.title: Required
docs.text: Key Description lake Run label: used in output file names and the Docker container name. algorithm Native: "EnKF" or "PF". OpenDA: "EnKF", "DEnKF", "EnSR" or "PF". The native "PF" is best-member selection, not a Bayesian particle filter (Workblog). n_members Ensemble size, at least 2. The members are ensemble1..N. ensemble0 is an unperturbed copy of the model inputs that the engines do not run. start_date, end_date Run window, ISO instants read as UTC (a plain date is its 00:00). Both engines, native and OpenDA, assimilate the observations in (start_date, end_date], each at its own hour, and the members' final state is at end_date. start_date must be the time of the warm-start snapshot. model_inputs_path The model setup with its dated warm start. Only read: everything the run writes goes under ensemble_base. ensemble_base Output folder: the members ensemble0..N, the perturbation chain state, the mean trajectory, the summary and the logs. obs_file Observation CSV with time, depth, value columns: the series to assimilate (see assimilator.observations for how to make it). perturbations or perturbations_file The forcing-perturbation calibration, inline ({"variables": {"U": {"phi", "sigma"}, "V": .., "GLOB": ..}}; a flat {"U": .., "V": .., "GLOB": ..} also works) or as a JSON path. perturbations wins if both are set.

docs.title: Engine and method
docs.text: Key Default Used by Description engine "python" all "python" (native engine) or "openda". model "simstrat" all Forward model, see assimilator.models and register_model. inflation 1.0 native EnKF Multiplies the ensemble anomalies before the update. 1.0 = off.

docs.title: Run window and ensemble
docs.text: Key Default Description rng_seed 42 Seeds the forcing noise and the EnKF observation perturbations. Draws are keyed by absolute time, so a run continued in slices reproduces a continuous run. reset false Starts from scratch: clears the AR(1) chain state (perturbation_state.json) and, in the native engines, the live snapshots, member outputs, mean trajectory and diagnostics. Leave it off for an operational continuation.

docs.title: Observation error
docs.text: Key Default Description sigma_obs sigma_default Observation error in °C: a number, or {"mixed": .., "stratified": ..} with stratified = May to October. Fitted with assimilator.fitting.sigma (python src/assimilate.py fit sigma); it is only valid for the obs_file it was fitted on (Workblog). sigma_default 0.5 Fallback when sigma_obs is not set. The log says when it is used. obs_min_days 1 OpenDA only. Drops depths with fewer days of data than this. openda_restart unset OpenDA only. A restart chain: each run continues from the ensemble the previous run saved, so an ensemble run in daily slices keeps its spread. {"dir": ..., "keep": 7, "cycle_max_days": 31}, all optional: the chain folder (default <openda_dir>/restart), how many restart files to keep, and the longest single OpenDA run of a catch-up. A call runs from the chain's end to end_date, every observation analysed at its own time; OpenDA is not started on a window without observations. See assimilator/openda/restart.py.

docs.title: Forcing perturbation
docs.text: Key Default Description sigma_scale 1.0 Multiplies the AR(1) noise σ of every channel, to widen or narrow the spread. Changing it cold-starts the perturbation chain. ref_year the model's Reference year of the forcing time axis (Simstrat: 1981).

docs.title: Output and runtime
docs.text: Key Default Used by Description results_dir Results_<algorithm> native Model output folder inside each member. par_file Settings_<algorithm>.par native Name of the per-member copy of Settings.par the engine runs. It is created once from Settings.par and not rewritten afterwards, so delete it from the members after changing results_dir. copy_skip ["Results", "ref"] all Folders of the model inputs not copied into the members. max_workers all members at once all Cap on members run in parallel. progress false (CLI: on in a terminal) all Progress bar. docker_dir, repo_dir not set all When both are set, Docker mount paths under repo_dir are rewritten to docker_dir, for setups where Docker sees the files under another path.

docs.title: OpenDA only
docs.text: Key Default Description openda_bin not set The bin/ folder of OpenDA 3.4.0. The engine builds the OpenDA environment from it, so nothing needs sourcing. Without it, an environment already set up in the shell is used. openda_native "linux64_gnu" OpenDA native-library folder under openda_bin. openda_dir openda_<model>_<lake>_<algorithm> next to ensemble_base OpenDA working folder for this run.

docs.title: Model runtime
docs.text:
Filled in from the model's defaults. Override them only to run a different Simstrat build.

Key Default Description simstrat_version "3.0.4" Tag of the eawag/simstrat Docker image. simstrat_binary /simstrat/build/simstrat Simstrat executable inside the container. simstrat_workdir /simstrat/run Where ensemble_base is mounted inside the container.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text:
python src/assimilate.py <command> ... — run python src/assimilate.py <command> -h for every option.

Command Does run [config.json] [--sim-dir --obs --perturbations --start --end --out ...] One run. Flags override the config file's keys; with flags only, algorithm defaults to EnKF, n_members to 20 and lake to the setup folder's name. --reset, --force-copy (re-copy the setup into the members), --skip-oda (OpenDA: prepare only), --no-progress, --log-file. summarize config.json Rebuild a finished run's summary CSV and skill JSON from its member outputs. preprocess raw.csv -o out.csv [--w-seiche H] [--hour H \| --hour-window LO-HI] [--depths ...] Raw sub-daily observations → the series to assimilate (assimilator.observations). fit filter\|hour\|sigma\|perturbation ... The offline fits (assimilator.fitting), from local files.

docs.title: Using the package from another program
docs.text:
import sys
sys.path.append("<path to this repository>/src")     # e.g. as a git submodule
import assimilator

result = assimilator.run(cfg)                              # same keys as above
assimilator.analysis_mean_state(cfg, "warm_start.dat")     # ensemble-mean analysis as a warm start

from assimilator.observations import preprocess            # raw -> assimilated series
from assimilator.fitting.sigma import fit_sigma             # and the other fits

A forward model other than Simstrat is added by subclassing assimilator.models.base.ForwardModel and calling assimilator.register_model(MyModel); the engines do not change. tests/toy_model.py is a complete minimal example.

docs.title: Literature review
docs.text:
In short

Five papers shaped the module. Baracchini et al. (2020) is the closest precedent: an EnKF with forcing perturbation, 20 members, on Lake Geneva. Safin et al. (2022) show the particle-filter alternative and its cost. Kourzeneva (2014) is the early 1D lake reference. Thomas et al. (2020) and Wander et al. (2024) come from the FLARE forecasting system and shaped how we think about uncertainty sources and assimilation frequency. Further reading follows at the end.

docs.title: Baracchini et al. (2020): EnKF for a 3D model of Lake Geneva
docs.text:
Baracchini, T., Chu, P. Y., Šukys, J., Lieberherr, G., Wunderle, S., Wüest, A., and Bouffard, D. (2020). Data assimilation of in situ and satellite remote sensing data to 3D hydrodynamic lake models: a case study using Delft3D-FLOW v4.03 and OpenDA v2.4. Geoscientific Model Development, 13(3), 1267–1284. doi:10.5194/gmd-13-1267-2020

Summary. A data assimilation framework that combines in situ profiles, satellite surface temperature and a 3D hydrodynamic model, built for near-real-time operation (meteolakes.ch). An EnKF in OpenDA assimilates in situ temperature profiles and AVHRR lake surface water temperature (LSWT) into Delft3D-FLOW for Lake Geneva.

Method. Delft3D-FLOW v4.03 (z-layer, 100 vertical levels, 450 m grid, κ-ε closure) coupled to OpenDA v2.4 through a file-based black-box wrapper, for 2017. The EnKF updates the 3D temperature state only. Spread is injected into the wind forcing (u and v), with OpenDA's spatiotemporally correlated noise model, whose standard deviation and correlation scales come from the COSMO-E ensemble. Assimilated: 31 in situ profiles at SHL2 and GE3, and 128 quality-filtered AVHRR images (of 3372). Observation error from instrument precision plus a 48-hour variability window for in situ data, and a 1 °C threshold for AVHRR. Gaspari–Cohn localization with a 15 km cutoff; an ensemble-size sensitivity study.

Results. RMSE −54 % and MAE −60 % against the calibrated control run, consistent from the surface to the deep water. A warm bias in the 5–25 m layer is removed and the thermocline depth corrected. Gyres, thermal fronts and upwellings are preserved and sharpened: a September upwelling underestimated by 5 °C is reduced to a 2.5 °C error. With localization, 20 members were enough.

Relevance for us. The closest precedent to our setup: forcing perturbation, state update, 20 members, operational aim. The starting point for the 3D extension.

docs.title: Safin et al. (2022): physics-preserving particle filter for Lake Geneva
docs.text:
Safin, A., Bouffard, D., Ozdemir, F., Ramon, C. L., Runnalls, J., Georgatos, F., Minaudo, C., and Šukys, J. (2022). A Bayesian data assimilation framework for lake 3D hydrodynamic models with a physics-preserving particle filtering method using SPUX-MITgcm v1. Geoscientific Model Development, 15(20), 7715–7730. gmd.copernicus.org/articles/15/7715/2022

Summary. A Bayesian framework coupling the inference package SPUX with MITgcm for Lake Geneva, positioned as an advance on Baracchini et al. (2020), which could use only about 3.7 % of the available LSWT images. Three components:

  1. Parameter inference with EMCEE, an affine-invariant ensemble sampler, suited to nonlinear parameters but expensive.
  2. A physics-preserving particle filter. Trajectories are resampled by their observational likelihood; states are only deleted or replicated, never modified, so there are no shocks.
  3. A BiLSTM network for the bulk-to-skin conversion, estimating skin temperature from 27 hours of bulk temperature and meteorology, with its uncertainty, so that nearly all quality-flagged pixels can be used.

Results. RMSE and MAE improve by only 4–15 %, but with 798 AVHRR images instead of about 124 and without image-by-image thresholding. The BiLSTM reduces RMSE by 33 % on its test set but increases it by about 10 % in the assimilation run. About 3 months on the Swiss National Supercomputing Centre. The authors suggest cheaper parameter optimisation plus an improved particle filter for operational use.

Relevance for us.

  • Small improvement over the control run, at a very high computational cost.
  • Particle filtering degenerates with dense, informative observations, as our PF does (Method).
  • Each member is driven by a COSMO-E ensemble member: a possible alternative to statistical forcing noise.
  • The bulk-to-skin observation operator is a template for satellite assimilation.

docs.title: Kourzeneva (2014): EKF for the 1D lake scheme FLake
docs.text:
Kourzeneva, E. (2014). Assimilation of lake water surface temperature observations using an extended Kalman filter. Tellus A: Dynamic Meteorology and Oceanography, 66(1), 21510. doi:10.3402/tellusa.v66.21510

Summary. An early and influential lake DA paper: an extended Kalman filter (EKF) assimilates lake water surface temperature into FLake, the two-layer parameterisation used in numerical weather prediction. The analysed variables are the mean water temperature, the bottom temperature, the mixed-layer depth and the shape factor.

Method. The small control vector of FLake makes an EKF tractable, an advantage over ensemble methods in NWP. Mixed and stratified regimes are treated separately, and the filter is re-initialised when the regime switches. Ice is handled implicitly: an observed surface temperature means no ice. Jacobians by finite differences, one perturbed FLake run per control variable. 27 Finnish lakes with in situ data, 4 with merged in situ and MODIS data.

Results. The free run has FLake's known summer warm bias, up to 5 °C in the mixed layer; the EKF brings it close to the observations on all 27 lakes. Satellite data help where in situ coverage is sparse. Little effect on ice, because observations are missing just before freeze-up. Spring and early-summer observations are the most valuable for the warming period.

Relevance for us. A simple 1D model with a known bias, corrected by assimilation of state variables without an ensemble.

docs.title: Thomas et al. (2020): FLARE and uncertainty partitioning
docs.text:
Thomas, R. Q., Figueiredo, R. J., Daneshmand, V., Bookout, B. J., Puckett, L. K., and Carey, C. C. (2020). A near-term iterative forecasting system successfully predicts reservoir hydrodynamics and partitions uncertainty in real time. Water Resources Research, 56(11), e2019WR026138. doi:10.1029/2019WR026138 · Code: FLAREr

Summary. FLARE (Forecasting Lake And Reservoir Ecosystems), a daily iterative forecasting system for Falling Creek Reservoir:

  • Sensors: a thermistor chain and an inflow sensor, streamed to the cloud.
  • Model: the 1D General Lake Model (GLM), driven by the 21 members of the NOAA GEFS 16-day forecast.
  • Filter: an EnKF that updates the temperature profile and three parameters (a longwave scaling factor and two sediment temperatures) by state augmentation.

Uncertainty partitioning, the main contribution. Five sources, each switchable on and off:

  • driver: one GEFS member per FLARE member;
  • initial condition: the spread on day 0;
  • process: Gaussian noise on the temperature at each daily step, correlated over depth;
  • parameter: spread of the three estimated parameters;
  • observation: sensor error in the EnKF's R.

Results. Skilful 16-day temperature forecasts in real time. Process and driver uncertainty dominate the forecast variance; initial conditions matter only at the shortest horizons. That is the opposite of weather forecasting, where initial conditions dominate. Running with fixed parameters degraded skill substantially.

Relevance for us. A 1D operational forecasting system, with ensembles of about 400 members for a light model. Process noise as a source of spread is the basis of our forecast uncertainty band.

docs.title: Wander et al. (2024): how often to assimilate
docs.text:
Wander, H. L., Thomas, R. Q., Moore, T. N., Lofton, M. E., Breef-Pilz, A., and Carey, C. C. (2024). Data assimilation experiments inform monitoring needs for near-term ecological forecasts in a eutrophic reservoir. Ecosphere, 15(2), e4752. doi:10.1002/ecs2.4752

Summary. If initial conditions are not the dominant uncertainty, how often do we need to assimilate? FLARE on Beaverdam Reservoir (0.28 km², 11 m deep, dimictic, eutrophic), 2021, with temperature sensors every metre. Assimilation daily, weekly, fortnightly or monthly, by withholding observations; forecasts 1 to 35 days ahead.

Method. GLM v3.3.0 driven by 30 NOAA GEFS members, 0.5 m vertical resolution. EnKF with 256 members and state augmentation of three parameters (longwave scaling, two sediment temperatures). Process noise 0.75 °C, observation noise 0.1 °C. Scored with RMSE (2 °C "skilful" threshold) and CRPS, separately for surface, middle and bottom layers and for mixed and stratified periods.

Results.

  • Frequency. Daily assimilation is best at 1–7 days, weekly at 8–35 days and overall. Daily assimilation crosses the 2 °C threshold by day 28; the others never do. Daily updates over-fit the parameters, which become noisier than with weekly updates. Fixed parameters with daily state updates are much worse (RMSE 3.12 against 1.95 °C).
  • Depth and season. Bottom waters are the most skilful (1.13 °C), the surface the least (1.78 °C); stratified slightly better than mixed. The horizon at which weekly overtakes daily is longer at depth (> 8 days) than at the surface (> 5 days).
  • Initial-condition share. With daily assimilation, initial conditions are 0.01 % of the 1-day forecast variance; with less frequent assimilation, 54–71 %. Beyond 10 days, below 1 % almost everywhere.
  • Parameters. Their spread had to be fixed a priori, because over a year the EnKF collapsed it.

Recommendations of the authors. Weekly observations are "good enough" for most uses; daily assimilation pays off for short horizons or for the hypolimnion in summer. Run withholding experiments before investing in high-frequency sensors.

Caveats. One reservoir, one year, one variable; daily was the finest frequency tested.

Relevance for us. Supports daily assimilation for short-horizon accuracy, and weekly assimilation for longer forecasts (When to assimilate).

docs.title: Further reading
docs.text:
Papers of wider or partial relevance.

Lakes and reservoirs

  • Baracchini, T., Hummel, S., Verlaan, M., Cimatoribus, A., Wüest, A., and Bouffard, D. (2020). An automated calibration framework and open source tools for 3D lake hydrodynamic models. Environmental Modelling & Software, 134, 104787. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2020.104787. Calibration as offline assimilation: Delft3D-FLOW and OpenDA coupled for automated parameter estimation, tested on Lake Geneva and Greifensee.
  • Kheyrollah Pour, H., Rontu, L., Duguay, C., Eerola, K., and Kourzeneva, E. (2014). Impact of satellite-based lake surface observations on the initial state of HIRLAM. Part II: Analysis of lake surface temperature and ice cover. Tellus A, 66, 21395. doi:10.3402/tellusa.v66.21395. Satellite lake surface temperature assimilated into the initial state of a weather model.
  • Chen, C., et al. (2019). Assimilating multi-source data into a three-dimensional hydro-ecological dynamics model using Ensemble Kalman Filter. Environmental Modelling & Software, 117, 188–199. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2019.03.028. An EnKF in a 3D hydro-ecological model (3DHED) for cyanobacterial biomass in Lake Taihu; adding remote sensing to the in situ data improves the spatial patterns.
  • Li, et al. (2022). Coupling remote sensing and particle tracking to estimate trajectories in large water bodies. EPFL Infoscience. Sentinel-2/3 suspended matter maps validate a Delft3D particle-tracking model of Lake Geneva, which in turn fills the gaps between overpasses.
  • Carey et al. (2024). A framework for developing a real-time lake phytoplankton forecasting system to support water quality management in the face of global change. Ambio. doi:10.1007/s13280-024-02076-7. A concept paper for an automated real-time forecasting system with quantified uncertainty, with DA as a central component.

Other domains

  • Javaheri et al. (2019). An adaptive ensemble Kalman filter for assimilation of multi-sensor, multi-modal water temperature observations into hydrodynamic model of shallow rivers. Journal of Hydrology. ScienceDirect. In situ sensors (dense in time) and Landsat-7 (dense in space) combined in an adaptive EnKF; deals with the skin–bulk temperature mismatch.
  • Miyazawa, Y., et al. (2013). Data assimilation of the high-resolution sea surface temperature obtained from the Aqua-Terra satellites (MODIS-SST) using an ensemble Kalman filter. Remote Sensing, 5(6), 3123–3139. doi:10.3390/rs5063123. An LETKF with spatiotemporally varying covariances for the Kuroshio front; quality control removes most of the cloud-induced cold bias, and the ensemble spread screens erroneous data. Relevant for 3D and satellite work later.
  • Wongchuig, S., et al. (2024). Multi-satellite data assimilation for large-scale hydrological-hydrodynamic prediction: proof of concept in the Amazon basin. Water Resources Research, 60(8). doi:10.1029/2024WR037155. A multi-observation local EnKF (MoLEnKF) for water surface elevation, water storage, flood extent and soil moisture; water surface elevation gives the largest gains (discharge error −38 %).
  • Cao, Y., et al. (2019). A modified particle filter-based data assimilation method for a high-precision 2-D hydrodynamic model considering spatial-temporal variability of roughness: simulation of dam-break flood inundation. Water Resources Research, 55. doi:10.1029/2018WR023568. Local weighting with spatially varying roughness improves all gauges, global weighting only a few.
  • Improving hydrodynamic modeling of river networks by incorporating data assimilation using a particle filter (2023). International Journal of Sediment Research, 38(5), 711–723. ScienceDirect. A particle filter for the Yangtze–Dongting river–lake network, comparing Gaussian and Cauchy likelihoods.
  • Batrak (2021). Implementation of an adaptive bias-aware extended Kalman filter for sea-ice data assimilation in the HARMONIE-AROME numerical weather prediction system. Ice surface temperature RMSE −0.4 °C and 2 m temperature −0.2 °C, persisting up to 24 h.

Reviews and tools

  • Cho, Pachepsky, Ligaray, Kwon and Kim (2020). Data assimilation in surface water quality modeling: a review. Water Research, 186, 116307. doi:10.1016/j.watres.2020.116307. DA methods in water quality modelling, factors affecting their performance (scale mismatch, data and model uncertainty), and open challenges.
  • Ridler et al. (2014). Data assimilation framework: linking an open data assimilation library (OpenDA) to a widely adopted model interface (OpenMI). Environmental Modelling & Software, 57, 76–89. doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2014.02.008. Technical integration of OpenDA, tested with an EnKF in MIKE SHE.

docs.title: Data Assimilation Framework for Operational Lake Modelling in Canton Ticino
docs.text:
James Runnalls, Eawag

Damien Bouffard, Eawag & UNIL

Martin Schmid, Eawag

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text: We propose developing a data assimilation framework to enhance the accuracy and reliability of operational one-dimensional (1D) lake models in Canton Ticino. This framework will integrate real-time observations with numerical models to improve predictions of lake thermal structure, providing water managers with more precise forecasting capabilities. Through its flexible, open-source architecture and scalable design, the framework will establish a standardized foundation for operational lake forecasting that can be deployed across Switzerland.

docs.title: Problem statement
docs.text:
While the operational models integrated into Alplakes successfully capture day-to-day variations in lake dynamics, they suffer from small inaccuracies, which can limit the use of such models. The errors result from:

  • Simplified physics and model parameters
  • Inaccurate forcing data (meteorology) that cannot accurately represent the conditions for the entire lake

We have two choices: focusing on consistency (continuous model runs) or accuracy (frequent re-initialization). Re-initializing models to match observations creates discontinuous jumps in the timeseries, breaking the physical consistency needed for trend analysis and scenario studies. Yet allowing models to run freely means accepting growing inaccuracy over time.

docs.title: The Missing Link: Data Assimilation
docs.text: To solve this challenge, we propose the use of a data assimilation tool that will create a continuous connection between models and observations, maintaining both accuracy and consistency over any timescale. Currently, the observation network and models operate in parallel but rarely communicate. Observations are used to validate model performance after the fact, but not to correct models during operation. This means we're not extracting full value from either investment—models don't benefit from real-time observations, and observations don't inform predictions beyond initial conditions.

docs.title: Current Operational Capabilities
docs.text:
Eawag and Canton Ticino have already invested significantly in lake monitoring and modelling infrastructure, providing the needed data and models to allow:

  • Providing lake hydrodynamic forecasting capabilities: 5-day predictions for planning and decision-making.
  • Providing continuous timeseries: Structured data pipeline and gap filling between observations with physically consistent estimates
  • Scenario analysis: Testing "what-if" situations for management decisions
  • Climate projections: Understanding long-term trends and impacts

Currently, the system integrates:

docs.title: In situ observation
docs.text:
• Operational in-situ monitoring network with temperature chains and meteorological stations deployed across major lakes
  • Automated data transmission and storage systems providing near real-time observations

docs.title: Satellite Data
docs.text:
• Routine acquisition of Landsat Collection 2 (Landsat-8, Landsat-9) thermal imagery
  • Processing chains for lake surface temperature and water quality parameters
  • Archive of historical satellite observations for validation

docs.title: Operational Models
docs.text:
• 1D hydrodynamic models (Simstrat) running daily for major lakes
  • Automated forecasting system producing 5-day predictions
  • Web-based visualization platform for model outputs (Alplakes)
  • Established workflows for model initialization and forcing data (Operational-Simstrat)

docs.title: Technical Infrastructure
docs.text:
• Dedicated computational resources for model simulations
  • REST API for managing observations and model outputs
  • Operational staff familiar with current systems

This existing infrastructure means we can focus resources entirely on developing and implementing the data assimilation layer, rather than building basic capabilities from scratch.

docs.title: Proposed Solution
docs.text: We will develop AlplakesDA - a modular, open-source Python library for operational lake data assimilation. This library will provide a production-ready toolkit that seamlessly integrates observations with lake models.

docs.title: Core Library Features
docs.text:
• Plug-and-play data assimilation for Simstrat (extendable to other models)
  • Automated observation processing from multiple sources (in-situ, satellite, meteorological)
  • Ensemble-based uncertainty quantification with configurable ensemble sizes
  • Real-time quality assurance for incoming observations
  • Flexible assimilation scheduling
  • Performance monitoring with validation metrics and diagnostic outputs

The library will be configuration-driven, requiring no code changes for operational adjustments.

docs.title: Modular Architecture
docs.text:
AlplakesDA will be organized into independent, replaceable modules:

  • Observation Handlers: Processors for satellite (Sentinel, Landsat), in-situ (CTD, thermistor chains), and meteorological data sources
  • Model Interfaces: Wrapper for Simstrat, with abstract base classes for easy addition of new models
  • Assimilation Core: OpenDA integration providing Ensemble Kalman Filter with localization and inflation
  • Quality Assurance: Comprehensive QA/QC including range checks, spike detection, spatial consistency tests, and climatological validation
  • Observation Operators: Tools for interpolation, averaging, and variable transformation between model and observation spaces
  • Diagnostics Suite: Validation metrics, visualization tools, and automated reporting

docs.title: OpenDA Integration
docs.text:
The library will leverage OpenDA, a proven open-source data assimilation platform used operationally worldwide. OpenDA provides robust, well-tested implementations of:

  • Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) with various flavors
  • Localization methods to handle spatially sparse observations
  • Parallel ensemble management for computational efficiency
  • Established interfaces to multiple modelling systems

docs.title: Quality Assurance Pipeline
docs.text:
All observations will pass through a multi-stage QA process:

  • Physical bounds checking (temperature, velocity ranges)
  • Temporal consistency analysis (spike and drift detection)

docs.title: Extensibility by Design
docs.text:
The modular structure ensures easy expansion:

  • New observation types: Drone measurements, citizen science data, or IoT sensors can be added by implementing standard interfaces
  • Additional models: 3D models (Delft3D, MITgcm) or other 1D models can be integrated through model wrappers
  • Alternative DA methods: Variational approaches or particle filters can be added alongside EnKF
  • Multiple lakes: Configuration files allow deployment to new water bodies without code modification

docs.title: Expected Impact
docs.text:
By adding data assimilation to our existing capabilities, we expect:

  • Significant reduction in model errors for lake temperature
  • Quantified uncertainty enabling risk-based decision-making
  • Reduced manual intervention through automated parameter updating
  • Increased usage of data by stakeholders due to improved reliability

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text: This project represents a logical and cost-effective evolution of Canton Ticino's lake monitoring and prediction capabilities. By adding data assimilation to our already-operational observation and modelling systems, we can dramatically improve forecast accuracy without duplicating infrastructure investments. The modular approach ensures that current operations continue uninterrupted while we enhance their capabilities.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text:
One assimilation run for one lake: what to install, which files to prepare, how to run, and what comes out. The examples use upperlugano; replace it with your lake.

The repository holds the code and an example configuration, but no model setups and no observations. Each user prepares those for their own lake. This page describes what the files must contain and how the operational ones were made; how you produce them is up to you. Operationally, operational-simstrat prepares all of them and calls the same assimilator.run(cfg) this page runs from the command line.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
• Python with numpy, pandas and tqdm (matplotlib for the plots, pytest for the tests).
  • Docker with the eawag/simstrat:3.0.4 image. Simstrat runs inside Docker, so nothing needs compiling.
  • For the OpenDA engine only: Linux or WSL, and OpenDA 3.4.0.

docs.title: 2. What a run needs
docs.text:
<setup folder>/                     Simstrat setup + warm-start snapshot      (read only)
<free run T_out.dat>                free run (only to fit sigma_obs and the hour)
<observations>.csv                  the observations to assimilate
<perturbations>.json                forcing-perturbation calibration
<config>.json                       one flat run configuration (optional: flags work too)

Where these files live is up to you; the paths go into the run configuration or on the command line. The examples below use inputs/<lake>/, observations/<lake>/ and run/<lake>/ inside the repository, which git ignores.

docs.title: 2.1 Simstrat setup: inputs/<lake>/
docs.text:
A complete, calibrated Simstrat setup that runs on its own: Settings.par, Forcing.dat, bathymetry, grid, initial conditions, absorption, inflow and outflow files, and z_out.dat. Setups for the Alplakes lakes can be downloaded from alplakes.eawag.ch/downloads. On top of a standard setup:

  • Settings.par must have "Continue from last snapshot" enabled, so each assimilation window restarts from the state the previous one left, and "Reference year" 1981 (SIMSTRAT_REF_YEAR in models/simstrat/model.py). The engines set the start and end dates themselves, in their own copies.
  • Forcing.dat is the standard Simstrat file: one header line, then time (days since 1 January of the reference year), u and v wind (m/s), air temperature (°C), solar radiation (W/m²), vapour pressure (mbar), cloud cover (–) and rain (m/h). It must cover the whole run. Each member gets its own copy with u, v and solar radiation perturbed.
  • z_out.dat lists the output depths. The run adds the observation depths to the members' copies, so you don't have to. The setup folder itself is never modified; the extended grid is written to <ensemble_base>/z_out.dat in case you want it for your own runs.

docs.title: 2.2 Warm-start snapshot and free run
docs.text:
Warm-start snapshot, inputs/<lake>/simulation-snapshot_<YYYYMMDD>.dat: the Simstrat snapshot of the model state at start_date. Every member starts from it. It comes from a spin-up: run Simstrat from its initial conditions up to start_date and keep the snapshot it writes at the end.

The date must match start_date exactly, and nothing checks it. A snapshot holds only the model state, not a time: the run takes its time from start_date, so a snapshot from another date is silently used as if it were the state at start_date. With several snapshots in the folder, the one with the latest date in its name is used, so keep only the one for the run.

Free run (e.g. inputs/<lake>/ref/T_out.dat): the same setup run over the assimilation period from the warm-start snapshot, with the control forcing, without perturbation and without assimilation. It is the reference that sigma_obs and the assimilation hour are fitted against (§2.3, §2.4), and the baseline the results are compared with. The run itself does not need it.

docs.title: 2.3 Observations: observations/<lake>/<file>.csv
docs.text:
A CSV in long format, one row per (time, depth). Leave out a missing reading rather than writing a row for it: an empty value is skipped, but a literal NaN is read by the OpenDA engine as a number. Several readings at the same depth within the same hour are averaged.

time,depth,value
2025-01-01T06:00:00+00:00,0.5,8.03
2025-01-01T06:00:00+00:00,1.0,7.96
Column Meaning time ISO 8601 with time zone, UTC. depth Metres below the surface, positive. value Temperature, °C.

Other columns are ignored. In particular, a quality flag is not applied: remove rejected readings before the run.

The file is the analysis schedule. Every distinct time in it becomes an analysis, so it must contain only the readings to assimilate. A raw record with a sample every 10 minutes would assimilate every hour. Readings are grouped into hourly bins centred on the full hour, and depths below the model's lake bed are dropped.

The operational files are made from the full sub-daily record in three steps, implemented in assimilator.observations and available as

python src/assimilate.py preprocess raw.csv -o observations/upperlugano/temperature_filtered_h06_1d.csv \
    --w-seiche 27.3 --hour 6                    # [--depths 0.5,1,3,...] [--hour-window 0-6]

Rows are only ever selected or averaged, never invented.

  1. Filter the internal-wave signal (fit filter --raw raw.csv --length-km L --mean-depth D derives the window). Below 4 m, most hour-to-hour variance is the thermocline being moved up and down by basin-scale seiches, which a 1D model cannot reproduce. Each depth below 4 m is replaced by a trailing (causal) mean over one fundamental internal-seiche period of the lake, from Merian's two-layer formula T = 2L / sqrt(g'·h_eff) at peak stratification: 11 h on Ägeri, 27 h on Upper Lugano, 97 h on Geneva. A value is dropped when its window is less than a quarter full or holds only samples from before a gap. The top 4 m pass through untouched. Same rows in and out.
  2. Choose the assimilation hour. Using the free run, split the surface error at each hour of the day into its mean over days (bias the model repeats every day) and its day-to-day scatter (error the analysis can correct). Among hours the lake samples on at least 30 days, keep those whose bias is at most 0.2 times their scatter, then take the one with the largest scatter. Candidates are limited to 00 to 06 UTC by default (--window, which may wrap, e.g. 23-6), so the analysis lands before the day it forecasts and every lake is corrected at a comparable point of its daily cycle. python src/assimilate.py fit hour --raw raw.csv --free-run T_out.dat does this.
  3. Thin to one profile per day. Each day, take the instant nearest the chosen hour and keep every depth at that instant. Drop the day if that instant is more than 1.5 h from the hour. For dense sensor chains, keep only the depths nearest a target grid (within 0.5 m): about 1 m spacing through the thermocline, opening to 5 m below it.

The reasons behind each step, and their effect on the results, are in the Workblog: Method and Experiments.

docs.title: 2.4 Observation error: sigma_obs
docs.text:
The observation error σ in °C, one value or one per season ({"mixed": .., "stratified": ..}, stratified = May to October). It stands for what the 1D model cannot represent, not for instrument error (Workblog). To fit it:

  1. take the free run minus the observations at the assimilated times;
  2. per depth and season, take the standard deviation about that season's own mean;
  3. take the median over depths.

python src/assimilate.py fit sigma --free-run T_out.dat --obs <the assimilated file> does this and prints the pair to put into the run configuration. σ belongs to the observation file it was fitted on: refit it whenever the filtering, the hour or the depth grid changes. Without it the run uses sigma_default (0.5 °C).

docs.title: 2.5 Forcing-perturbation calibration
docs.text:
The AR(1) noise added to the forcing (Workblog and calibration): {"variables": {"U": {"phi", "sigma"}, "V": .., "GLOB": ..}}, as a JSON file or inline in the configuration. The calibrations of the seven study lakes are kept by operational-simstrat (static/assimilation/<lake>.json, key perturbations); examples/enkf.json carries upperlugano's.

The math is in assimilator.fitting.perturbation. The amplitude needs the ICON reanalysis lake mean (Eawag network), so that fit is run from operational-simstrat (src/assimilation_tools/fit_perturbation.py). The persistence ceiling needs only the control forcing:

python src/assimilate.py fit perturbation --sim-dir inputs/upperlugano --existing upperlugano.json -o upperlugano.json

The run stops if no calibration is given.

docs.title: 2.6 Run configuration
docs.text:
One flat JSON per run; examples/enkf.json is a complete one:

{
    "lake": "upperlugano", "algorithm": "EnKF", "n_members": 20,
    "start_date": "2025-01-01", "end_date": "2025-12-31",
    "model_inputs_path": "inputs/upperlugano",
    "ensemble_base": "run/upperlugano",
    "obs_file": "observations/upperlugano/temperature_filtered_h06_1d.csv",
    "sigma_obs": {"mixed": 0.299, "stratified": 0.586},
    "perturbations_file": "upperlugano.json"
}

start_date must be the date of the warm-start snapshot (§2.2). Relative paths resolve against the directory you run from. Every key is described in Configuration.

docs.title: 3. Run
docs.text:
python src/assimilate.py run examples/enkf.json
# or without a config file:
python src/assimilate.py run --sim-dir inputs/upperlugano --obs obs.csv --perturbations upperlugano.json \
    --start 2025-01-01 --end 2025-12-31 --out run/upperlugano

The log goes through five steps:

  1. check that the Simstrat setup and the snapshot are there;
  2. copy the setup into the members (skipped if already done; --force-copy repeats it);
  3. write a perturbed Forcing.dat into each member;
  4. run the members window by window, assimilating at each observation time;
  5. write the results and a skill report.

The console shows a progress bar; the full log is in <ensemble_base>/logs/pipeline_<timestamp>.log. "algorithm": "PF" (or --algorithm PF) runs best-member selection instead. "engine": "openda" runs the same experiment through the OpenDA engine; for it alone, set openda_bin to the bin/ folder of your OpenDA installation.

Continuing a run. With "reset": false, running again with a later end_date carries on where the last run stopped. All random draws are tied to absolute time, so the result is the same as one continuous run. "reset": true starts from scratch.

docs.title: 4. Outputs
docs.text:
Native engine, in ensemble_base:

File Content <lake>_python_<algorithm>.csv Ensemble mean and standard deviation per time and depth. <lake>_python_<algorithm>.json RMSE and bias (model minus observation) against the assimilated observations, overall and per depth. T_out_<algorithm>_mean.dat Ensemble-mean trajectory in Simstrat's T_out format; the algorithm in lower case, e.g. T_out_enkf_mean.dat. enkf_diagnostics.csv, enkf_innov_by_depth.csv, enkf_kgain_by_depth.csv Native EnKF only. Innovations, spread, NIS and gain per analysis, tracked to analyse how the filter behaves; the run itself does not use them. ensemble<i>/<results_dir>/ Each member's Simstrat output.

OpenDA writes the same CSV and JSON, named <lake>_openda_<algorithm>.*, in openda_dir (default: openda_simstrat_<lake>_<algorithm>/ next to ensemble_base).

The skill report scores the analysis against the observations it assimilated: it measures fit, not independent skill. For an honest check, compare against data the run did not see. python notebooks/visualize.py <config>.json --free-run T_out.dat --save plots a run and compares it with the free run.

docs.title: Experiments
docs.text:
Last updated: November 2026. Unless stated otherwise: 2025, 20 members, native EnKF, operational setup apart from the one thing each experiment changes.

In short

Every experiment we ran, what it asked, and what came of it. Daily assimilation, seiche filtering and profile data pay off. Making σ more refined makes the filter better calibrated, not more accurate. Surface-only assimilation damages the layers below. Extra spread from model parameters helps a little at daily steps, but only at amplitudes we cannot defend; at longer steps it pays off. Assimilation leaves the model's natural variability intact.

The more recent work is promising: oxygen can be assimilated together with temperature, with large gains where the profiler covers the column; centring the forcing ensemble removes a systematic windiness of the members; and learning the observation and model errors online makes the ensemble honest. Over 7-day forecasts, a more realistic wind perturbation (lake wind, slow wind noise) pays off where it does not in daily assimilation. Deep mixing remains open.

✅ Operational · (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · ⚙️ Optional · ❌ Tested, not adopted · 🔬 Open

Experiment Question Outcome Status Assimilation frequency Daily, or less often? Daily is best (Upperlugano pooled RMSE): −26 % vs −23 % (3 days) and −20 % (7 days) ✅ daily Observation filtering Does seiche filtering help? Yes: without it, hard to see gains at the thermocline ✅ Surface-only Is a surface station enough? No. Helps the surface, damages 10–35 m against CTD ❌ Depth-resolved σ Should σ vary with depth? Better shape and distribution, same accuracy; fitted on the free run, more complex, its generalization is questionable ❌ Rescaled σ Can σ be fitted to the filter's own innovations iteratively? NIS ≈ 1 everywhere, accuracy unchanged, even more complex and less generalizable ❌ Fitting year Does fitting σ on 2025 bias our results? Barely: gain within 1.5 points, the method is not very sensitive and can be used also on unseen years ✅ passes Adaptive σ Can σ follow the innovations on the fly? NIS ≈ 1 by construction, but it blames every miss on the observations: six of seven lakes less accurate, Ägeri runs away. Replaced by the learned R and q ❌ Learned R and q Can R and a model error be learned online instead, so the ensemble spread is honest? Yes, with one parameter: RMSE 0.612 → 0.584 °C, CRPS 0.313 → 0.246, spread/RMSE 0.26 → 0.98 (filtered observations). 7-day reforecasts from it are the next step 🔬 Ägeri check Does the method avoid the adaptive σ runaway, and what do the R split and q add? Yes: all to R 0.301, split 0.290 (but over-confident, NIS 1.76), split + q 0.275 °C (free run 0.461, simplified_final 0.299) ✅ Vertical localization Are spurious correlations the problem at depth? Small gains only, no clear advantage in using operationally for now, but potentially useful in the future on a different setup or application (✅) Parameter sensitivity Could parameters add spread at depth? Yes: ±1 °C at 11 m in summer 🔬 Parameter perturbation Does perturbing them help the filter? Daily: only slightly, and at amplitudes we cannot defend. With a longer assimilation step, though, it helps: every 3 days, p_lw ±10 % brings the accuracy back to close to the daily result (✅) Joint estimation Can the filter estimate the parameters? They don't converge, but absorb the seasonal bias; that could be useful for studying the model's systematic weaknesses 🔬 Deep mixing: Lugano & Geneva Can CTD assimilation fix deep mixing? Temperature (and oxygen) improve (Lugano 30–100 m 0.29 → 0.16 °C; Geneva 1.19 → 0.87 °C, O₂ 105 → 38). Mixing no: more frequent on Lugano (uncentred forcing), unchanged and still too frequent on Geneva (tested centred) 🔬 3D model Does the layout transfer to Delft3D? Yes, with promising first results (✅) Natural variability Does DA disturb the model's own oscillations? No: same spectral shape, one clean step per update ✅ passes Oxygen: assimilation, depth thinning & CTD interpolation Can O₂ be assimilated with T, from how few depths, and from casts alone? Profilers: Ägeri O₂ −45 %, Murten −18 %; the bottom boundary is a model problem. 5 of 23 depths keep ~35–40 % of the T gain, ~70 % of the O₂ gain. Monthly casts: good between casts in the deep water only (✅) Centred forcing Does the forcing noise bias the ensemble mean? Yes: mean wind speed +31 to +63 %; centring removes it (✅)

docs.title: Assimilation frequency
docs.text:
Status: ✅ Operational (daily) · Lakes: Upper Lugano

Question: How much accuracy is lost by assimilating less often than daily?

Setup: Same run at daily, 3-day and 7-day frequency, scored against hourly buoy data.

Result: The free run's 0.83 °C drops to 0.61 °C (−26 %) with daily assimilation (365 profiles), 0.64 °C (−23 %) every 3 days (122 profiles) and 0.67 °C (−20 %) every 7 days (53 profiles).

Verdict: Daily outperforms the lower frequencies we tested (Method).

Note: With more model spread, lower frequencies may catch up: with p_lw ±10 %, 3-day assimilation almost matches the daily result (Parameter perturbation).

Reproduce: feat/da-combi: notebooks/generate_assimilation_series.py --every-days N.

docs.title: Observation filtering
docs.text:
Status: ✅ Operational · Lakes: Upper Lugano

Question: What does the seiche filtering (Method) actually gain?

Setup: Assimilation in 2025 on unfiltered vs filtered observations, both scored (pooled RMSE °C over the year) against the same raw hourly data.

Figure 1. Upper Lugano 2025: RMSE by depth with assimilation of unfiltered (left) and filtered (right) observations, scored against the same raw hourly observations.

Result: Without filtering (Figure 1, left) almost nothing is achieved at the thermocline, and the red fill around 13 and 17 m says it was made slightly worse: the filter is chasing a signal it cannot represent and fails to inject it into the simulation. With filtering (right) we get an improvement everywhere.

Verdict: The data becomes more meaningful, and more digestible, for the filter and we get the hoped-for improvement at intermediate depths. All other results use filtered observations.

Reproduce: feat/da-combi: notebooks/calibrate_filter.py, notebooks/filter_observations.py.

docs.title: Surface-only assimilation
docs.text:
Status: ❌ Tested, not adopted · Lakes: Lower Lugano, Lower Zürich (plus Upper Lugano with surface data only)

Question: Several lakes have a surface station and nothing else. Is assimilating the surface enough?

Setup: Two lake sections where only surface data is available, with the same seasonal σ recipe applied to the single surface depth: Lower Lugano 0.41 °C mixed / 0.61 °C stratified, Lower Zürich 0.65 / 0.88 °C.

Figure 2. Surface-only assimilation through 2025 at 1 m: Lower Zürich and Lower Lugano, free run vs assimilation.

Result at the surface: Both lakes improve at the assimilated depth of 1 m, but very unequally. Lower Lugano 0.90 → 0.58 °C (−35 %); Lower Zürich 0.80 → 0.68 °C (−15 %). The difference most likely comes from the error each free run makes, not from the filter. Each correction is the innovation (observation minus forecast) times a gain, and that gain stays small when the ensemble is narrow compared with σ. Our setup has a fairly narrow ensemble and a large σ, so a correction can only be large when the error is large. When the free-run error stays low, the corrections are small and hard to see. Zürich's error is low (around 0.4 °C) for most of the year, with only short large excursions, so the filter has less to correct over the year. In January–February, and also in November–December for Zürich, the assimilated and free-run curves in Figure 2 are indistinguishable. The difference appears in March for Lugano and April for Zürich and lasts through the stratified season.

Figure 3. RMSE against CTD casts: surface-only assimilation, Lower and Upper Lugano (left), and full-profile assimilation, Upper Lugano (right).

Result in the column: Figure 3, left: Lower and Upper Lugano with surface-only assimilation; right: Upper Lugano assimilating the full profile. Both scored against CTD casts, a sub-optimal reference: casts are instantaneous and very exposed to the variability problem described in Method, while our assimilation works on filtered daily values, and the two panels are different lake sections. Surface-only gains at the top and, weakly, in the deep in lower Lugano. Similar results are obtained when assimilating the upper Lake Lugano section with surface measurements only (note: deep results change). Between them it loses badly: the RMSE degrades by up to 0.65 °C between roughly 10 and 35 m, more than the 0.4 °C it gains at the surface.

Profile assimilation gains almost everywhere down to 60 m, up to 0.7 °C at the surface, and below that does essentially nothing, within 0.02 °C of the free run all the way to 280 m.

Alternatives tried: The model is 1D, so no matter how many stations report, the filter must be handed one value per depth. The freedom is in how that value and its uncertainty are constructed. We tried defining σ from the observations alone rather than from the model gap: when the spread between stations is large (from climatology), trust the value less; when a value is derived from more stations at run time, trust it more. We tried localizing the corrections (Localization), and arbitrarily prescribing a low σ of 0.3 °C. The results change only at the surface and none of them improved the comparison against the CTD profiles at depth.

Verdict: Profile assimilation shows clearly better gains against CTD, and it appears to do little harm where it has no information; having profile information over the whole upper 30–40 m seems to be essential for correcting a 1D model.

Reproduce: feat/multi-station-obs: Lower Lugano and Lower Zürich setups, notebooks/sigma_rep_from_obs.py.

docs.title: Observation σ
docs.text:
A single fixed σ by season (Method) is simple, well suited to operational use, and already gives significant improvement across the year and the water column. But the simple recipe has clear drawbacks, and each one suggests a fix:

  • Seasonal aggregation assumes a clean mixed/stratified split, at the same calendar dates, across lakes and years. A finer temporal resolution (say monthly) would need more history than we have, and monthly conditions vary a lot from year to year.
  • Thermocline layers in summer remain challenging to assimilate.
  • Deep observations are trusted far too little, because their true representativeness error is much smaller than the depth-median σ.

In the tables below, "calibration" is the pooled NIS: 1 is perfectly consistent, below 1 over-cautious, above 1 over-confident.

docs.title: Depth-resolved σ
docs.text:
Status: ❌ Tested, not adopted · Lakes: all seven

Question: Does σ resolved by depth, instead of collapsed to a median, do better?

Setup: Same fitting concept, resolved by depth.

lake gain, simple gain, σ(z) NIS simple (all / mixed / strat.) NIS σ(z) (all / mixed / strat.) upperlugano −26.3 % −25.5 % 0.55 / 0.73 / 0.51 0.56 / 0.68 / 0.52 maggiore −28.5 % −28.4 % 0.87 / 0.38 / 1.04 0.91 / 0.38 / 1.13 greifensee −27.1 % −28.5 % 0.63 / 0.55 / 0.64 0.65 / 0.41 / 0.73 geneva −42.5 % −41.8 % 1.07 / 1.54 / 0.98 0.62 / 1.18 / 0.55 aegeri −35.2 % −28.5 % 0.94 / 0.66 / 1.14 0.75 / 0.63 / 0.79 hallwil −49.2 % −50.6 % 1.00 / 0.54 / 1.46 0.62 / 0.41 / 0.79 murten −34.2 % −30.9 % 0.60 / 0.96 / 0.50 0.62 / 0.66 / 0.59

Result: The structure of the budget looks visibly better: σ now follows the shape of the innovation profile instead of cutting across it. But the overall calibration stays about the same, because fixing the shape redistributes the misfit rather than removing it (the budget is more evenly distributed, not better in the pool). And the RMSE gain barely moves, while on Ägeri it gets notably worse (−35.2 → −28.5 %). The level stays too high for the same reason as in the seasonal σ of simplified_final: σ is still fitted on the free run's errors, and the purpose of assimilation is to make exactly those errors smaller, so the filter only ever sees smaller innovations than the ones σ was fitted on if assimilation works (Rescaled σ).

Verdict: The depth fit changes the shape of the uncertainty profile but not its level, and it brings no gain over the seasonal σ: for the moment we see no reason to use it. Fixing the level is the next experiment.

Reproduce: feat/da-combi: src/assimilator/sigma_rep.py, notebooks/fit_sigma_gap.py.

docs.title: Rescaled σ
docs.text:
Status: ❌ Tested, not adopted · Lakes: all seven

Question: The depth fit had the right shape and the wrong amplitude. Does fixing the level help?

Setup: Since the free-run fit sets σ generally too high (above), we take a previous run's uncertainty profile and rescale it against that run's own innovations, with four numbers per lake to keep the risk of overfitting as low as possible: above and below 4 m (where the seiche filtering starts), for each of the two seasons.

Figure 4. Uncertainty budget with depth-resolved σ (left) and rescaled σ (right), Upper Lugano 2025.

lake gain, σ(z) gain, scaled NIS σ(z) (all / mixed / strat.) NIS scaled (all / mixed / strat.) upperlugano −25.5 % −26.9 % 0.56 / 0.68 / 0.52 0.91 / 0.96 / 0.89 maggiore −28.4 % −25.7 % 0.91 / 0.38 / 1.13 1.13 / 0.87 / 1.16 greifensee −28.5 % −30.5 % 0.65 / 0.41 / 0.73 0.93 / 0.93 / 0.93 geneva −41.8 % −41.9 % 0.62 / 1.18 / 0.55 0.97 / 1.02 / 0.96 aegeri −28.5 % −28.6 % 0.75 / 0.63 / 0.79 1.00 / 0.94 / 1.01 hallwil −50.6 % −49.9 % 0.62 / 0.41 / 0.79 1.05 / 1.01 / 1.07 murten −30.9 % −32.8 % 0.62 / 0.66 / 0.59 0.94 / 0.99 / 0.91

Result: Figure 4 compares the two budgets on Upper Lugano. As a calibration test this works very well, as expected: every lake lands close to 1. Spring and winter remain hard in opposite directions, which is the price of the remaining two-season approximation. The RMSE gains move only a little, some up, some down, and the simple setup still beats this calibrated version in several cases: Some general tendencies are nonetheless visible. Calibration tends to score worse in spring, and that loss sits mainly at the surface. The depth-fitted experiments, on the other hand, tend to score better in deeper water and, for the scaled fit, in the winter months. At the thermocline we cannot generalise: of the two lakes with the largest losses there, Greifensee improves, closing part of its intermediate-depth degradation, while Ägeri gets worse.

Verdict: Filter self-consistency and filter accuracy are separate objectives: calibrating does not guarantee any improvement in performance. Calibration can offer a targeted repair at difficult depths and times, but not a reliable one. How well more complex or iterative fits would generalise to other years with the limited data at our disposal also remains questionable.

Reproduce: feat/da-combi: src/assimilator/sigma_rep.py, notebooks/fit_scale_by_depth.py.

docs.title: Fitting year
docs.text:
Status: ✅ Passes · Lakes: Ägeri, Hallwil, Greifensee

Question: The seasonal σ is independent of the filter, but not of the evaluation data: it was fitted on 2025, and every result here is scored on 2025. Does that matter? (2025 is the only year with profile observations on all seven lakes.)

Setup: Three lakes also have full records for 2023 and 2024 on an unchanged sensor chain. For those we refitted σ on 2023–24 and scored the result on 2025, changing nothing else.

lake σ fitted on 2025 σ fitted on 2023–24 RMSE gain, 2025 fit RMSE gain, 2023–24 fit aegeri 0.24 0.27 −35.2 % −34.3 % hallwil (mixed / strat.) 0.41 / 0.39 0.33 / 0.53 −49.2 % −47.7 % greifensee (mixed / strat.) 0.52 / 0.94 0.52 / 0.91 −27.1 % −27.6 %

Result: The fitted values do move between years, by up to a third (Hallwil's stratified season, odd case mentioned earlier). The result barely does. The gain changes by at most 1.5 points, and no depth differs by more than 0.03 °C. Hallwil's calibration even improves.

Verdict: Where it can be tested, the choice of fitting year matters much less than one might think and the recipe itself. Two caveats: the test covers three lakes and one scored year, and the forcing perturbation is still the one fitted on 2025, because the ICON reanalysis it needs does not reach back to 2024.

Reproduce: master at 20564a9: notebooks/generate_sigma.py, fitted on 2023–24 (now assimilate.py fit sigma).

docs.title: Learning the errors online
docs.text:
The σ fits above are made offline, on a reference year, and assume that year stands for the next ones. Here the errors are learned instead from the filter's own misses (innovations) as the run goes. It is one method with two switches (R_rule and q in pn_online), so three levels:

All to R R split R split + model error Switches R_rule: consistency, q: false R_rule: split, q: false R_rule: split, q: true Observation error R every excess miss: R² ← gap² − spread² only the part of the miss that does not repeat from day to day as R split Model error none none q, learned from the misses, added as daily noise on the profile Ensemble spread too small too small follows the error Ägeri 2025: RMSE / NIS (free run 0.461, simplified_final 0.299 / 0.98) 0.301 / 0.91 (first version: 0.398) 0.290 / 1.76 0.275 / 0.67 Upper Lugano 2025: RMSE (simplified_final 0.612) first version: gain −27 % against −26 % – 0.584

RMSE against the raw hourly observations, NIS from the filter (scoring).

docs.title: Adaptive σ
docs.text:
Status: ❌ Replaced by the learned R and q · Lakes: all seven; CTD check on Upper Lugano

Question: Can σ follow the innovations as the run goes, with no free run, seasonal split or iterative fit?

Setup: At each depth, σ² is the mean squared innovation minus the mean ensemble spread² over the 14 days before each analysis, σ(z,t)² = gap² − spread², with a 0.05 °C floor. The seasonal σ is used for the first 14 days, until the window fills.

Figure 5. Adaptive σ actually used, native EnKF vs OpenDA chain, against the seasonal σ, Upper Lugano 2025.

Result: On Upper Lugano σ climbs through the spring warming at the surface and peaks at the thermocline in October; below 25 m it falls well under the seasonal value (Figure 5). NIS is 1, as the estimator is built to produce, but the pooled RMSE barely moves (−26 → −27 %). The gain sits where the seasonal σ distrusted the observations (e.g. 30 m), and the 23 CTD casts, never assimilated, confirm it (better at 98 of 121 levels in the top 60 m). On the seven lakes NIS ends near 1 everywhere, but only Upper Lugano gets more accurate: the others lose a few points, and Ägeri loses more than half its gain (−35.2 → −13.6 %).

Ägeri shows the failure mode: from July to October the error grows between 10 and 20 m, at the thermocline (Figure 10). The estimator cannot tell whether a large miss comes from the measurement or from the model, so it always blames the observations. When the model starts misplacing the thermocline the misses grow, σ there climbs from 0.2 to 0.9 °C, the filter stops correcting that depth, and the error keeps growing.

Verdict: A self-tuning error model can look perfectly calibrated while degrading accuracy. It leaves two problems, which the next experiment answers: σ takes every miss, also the persistent ones that come from the model, and the ensemble spread stays as small as before.

Reproduce: adaptive_sigma: the adaptive_sigma config block, native engine and OpenDA restart chain; operational_openda-restart: src/assimilator/openda/restart.py, the openda_restart config block.

docs.title: Learned R and q: an honest uncertainty band
docs.text:
Status: 🔬 Analysis done; 7-day reforecasts are the next step · Lakes: Upper Lugano, 2025

In short

  • The operational setup is too confident. In simplified_final the ensemble spread is a quarter of the error (spread/RMSE 0.26). Its band only looks right because of one large, fixed observation error (0.30 °C in winter, 0.59 °C in summer, at every depth).
  • R and the model error q can be learned online from the filter's own misses, with one parameter (a ~20-day memory) and no tables to fit per lake.
  • Slightly more accurate, and honest: RMSE 0.612 → 0.584 °C, CRPS 0.313 → 0.246 °C, and the spread follows the error every month (spread/RMSE 0.98 against the filtered observations).
  • What it learns is physical: R peaks at 0.4 °C at 9 m in summer (internal waves) and stays at the sensor error in winter and at depth; q is largest near the surface in summer.

Question: Adaptive σ left two problems: it blames every miss on the observations, so a drifting model is answered by trusting the data less (the Ägeri runaway), and the ensemble spread stays far smaller than the error (Open problems). Can R be learned so that it takes only what really is observation error, and the rest be carried by the ensemble as a model error q?

Idea: three sources, kept apart. R is what a 1D lake-mean model cannot represent (sensor noise, internal waves). q is what it represents but gets wrong, added as a daily noise on the temperature profile, as in FLARE (Thomas et al., 2020). Bias is neither, and is not put into either. R and q are learned from the misses d = observation − forecast, with two standard rules.

Rule Why it works Reference q (daily model error) Each day q² moves by 5 % of (d² − spread² − R²) On average the miss must be as large as predicted, d² = spread² + R². Misses too large → q up, too small → q down Innovation consistency (Mehra 1970; Li et al. 2009) R (observation error) Each day R² moves by 5 % of (d_a·d − d·d_next), using yesterday's miss d, its post-analysis miss d_a and today's miss d_next, at the same depth Observation noise is new every day, model error persists: if misses repeat from day to day, the filter trusts the observations too little. R is right when they stop repeating Kailath 1968; Mehra 1970; Desroziers et al. 2005 Memory λ = 0.95 Each day counts 5 %, about the last 20 days dominate Longer than single events, shorter than the seasons. λ = 0.98 (~50 days) gives the same skill (RMSE 0.585, coverage 0.93) –

The rest of the setup, and how each part is done:

  • Shape of the noise in depth (fixed). Only the size q is learned per depth; how errors at different depths move together is a fixed correlation, one for the mixed and one for the stratified season, measured from the free run's day-to-day error. It matches the correlation of the run's own misses (e.g. 1–3 m 0.70 vs 0.76; 9–13 m in summer −0.29 vs −0.26, the thermocline moving up or down), so it is representative for this lake (and year for now).
  • Gross errors. An observation whose miss is more than 5 standard deviations (NIS > 25) is not assimilated, but still counts when q is learned, so a q that is too small cannot reject the very misses that should raise it.
  • No shift of the mean. Each day's noise is centred across members, so it adds spread without moving the ensemble mean.
  • Stable profiles. After the noise, any density inversion in a member is merged into its volume-weighted mean, so the heat content is unchanged. Only what the noise can cause is touched: 0–50 m (the noise reaches the deepest observation at 40 m and fades to zero over the next 10 m) and inversions larger than 0.001 kg/m³ (about 0.01 °C; the model's own are smaller).
  • Start. R starts at the sensor error (0.05 °C, also its lower limit) and learns only after 15 days, while the ensemble builds its spread; q starts at 0.

Result (daily DA, 2025):

Run RMSE (°C) CRPS (°C) spread / RMSE 90 % band incl. R spread only Free run 0.831 – – – – simplified_final (fixed σ, no noise) 0.612 0.313 0.26 (0.15) 0.95 (0.88) 10–40 % (10–40 %) Learned R and q (pn_online) 0.584 0.246 0.98 (0.43) 0.94 (0.79) 80–90 % (55–85 %) to 25 m

Upper Lugano 2025. RMSE and CRPS against the raw hourly buoy observations; spread/RMSE and the bands against the filtered observations at the 16 assimilated depths, raw in brackets (scoring). "Spread only": share of observations inside mean ± 1.645 × spread, the part of the band a forecast carries.

Both bands contain about 90 % of the observations, but for different reasons. Against the raw readings the learned band covers less (79 % against 88 %): its R describes the filtered reading, and the internal-wave signal the filtering removes is in neither the spread nor R. The simplified_final band is almost all fixed observation error: ±1 °C at 25–40 m, where the lake changes by hundredths, and so large that the deep water is barely corrected (25 m stays ~0.3 °C too warm, close to the free run). The learned band is tight where the lake is calm and wide where it is not (Figure 6), and its spread matches the error month by month (Figure 7). The learned R has a clear depth structure, unlike the single fixed value (Figure 8), and both R and q follow the seasons (Figure 9): R stays at the sensor error in winter and at 40 m and rises to about 0.5 °C at 9 m in summer, where internal waves move the thermocline; q is largest at 1 and 9 m from spring to September and drops to about 0 at 40 m after May. Inversions stay within what the free run produces itself (below 3 m, at most 1.9 % of hours in July, against 5.5 % in the free run).

Figure 6. Upper Lugano 2025: hourly filtered observations, free run, and the ensemble mean with its 90 % band for the buoy reading, mean ± 1.645 √(spread² + R²), for simplified_final and the learned R and q, at 1, 9, 25 and 40 m in spring onset, summer and autumn cooling. Under each panel, the share of observations inside each band.

Figure 7. Upper Lugano 2025, against the filtered observations at the 16 assimilated depths: (left) monthly RMSE of the ensemble mean (solid) against the ensemble spread (dashed): spread ≈ RMSE means an honest band; (right) coverage of the 90 % band by depth, with R (solid) and spread only (dashed).

Figure 8. Upper Lugano 2025, median over each season: (left) observation error R, learned (blue) against the fixed σ of simplified_final (orange); (right) the learned daily model error q. simplified_final has no model error.

Figure 9. Upper Lugano 2025, at 1, 9, 25 and 40 m: (top) observation error R, learned (blue) against the fixed σ of simplified_final (orange), dotted line the 0.05 °C sensor error; (bottom) the learned daily model error q. The first 15 days (warm-up) are not shown.

Limits:

  • The R/q split is defined by persistence. Internal waves lasting several days count as model error, so at 5 m R is smaller than an observation-based estimate.
  • q falls slowly after active periods. It rises within 2–3 weeks but takes 6–7 weeks to come down, because a calm day can lower it only a little and the ensemble keeps its spread. The band is wider than needed in autumn (98–100 % of observations inside).
  • Large corrections at the thermocline: without a step cap, 18 analyses move the water below 4 m by more than 1 °C (largest 2.0 °C). On Ägeri the same happens, less often: 3 analyses above 1 °C (largest 1.4 °C at 4 m in April), and the run is still the most accurate at those depths. The extra spread from q makes the filter trust the observations more, so it corrects in bigger steps. If the aim is to keep jumps and shocks to the model small, the R-only versions are decisively better: on Ägeri no correction exceeds 0.8 °C with the R split, or 0.43 °C with all to R.
  • Deep water in summer: q drops to 0 at 30–40 m, so the spread-only band covers 45–70 % there (errors of a few hundredths of a degree).
  • One year, in sample: Each depth learns q on its own, so the winter profile of q is noisy. A second lake is checked below.
  • The depth correlation is measured on 2025 only: Pooling more years as the record grows (2024–2026 now available) will make it a lake property rather than a property of one year.

Verdict: Learned R and q could be an automatic method to run the analysis: as accurate or slightly better than the operational setup (−5 % RMSE, −21 % CRPS against the raw observations), honest about its uncertainty, physically interpretable, one parameter, and standard references for each step.

Still to do: score it against the 23 Upper Lugano CTD casts, as adaptive σ. The run on Ägeri is the next section.

Next step: 7-day reforecasts. The band has only been tested in the daily cycle (0–24 h).

  1. Rerun the learned R and q with the analysis states saved every 7 days, then run weekly 7-day reforecasts from them with the observed weather, and score them by lead time against persistence and the free run (CRPS, RMSE, coverage).

  2. What to look for:

    • coverage stays near 90 % from day 1 to day 7 (below: q too small in forecasts; above: too large, e.g. in autumn);
    • whether the seasonal surface bias (summer too warm, spring too cold) still dominates the day-7 error;
    • whether the forecast ideas below improve the surface at longer leads.

  3. Real weather: archive the ICON ensemble forecasts (lake mean, per member and lead) and repeat with them as forcing, each DA member paired with one weather member. With the observed weather the band is a lower bound; this step makes it a forecast band. Check that the band is not too wide at long leads (q partly absorbs forcing error that the weather ensemble then also carries).

Ideas to improve the forecasts (to test with the reforecasts). Exploratory reforecasts from an earlier, hand-tuned version point to two ideas. Treat them as hypotheses to confirm, not results:

  • Lake wind. From June to October the station wind used as forcing is 12–25 % weaker than the wind measured on the lake (Castagnola buoy). Idea: scale the forecast wind by the buoy/model ratio of the previous weeks. Look for: a lower surface error at days 3–7 in summer, where the seasonal bias dominates.
  • Wind spread. The members' wind is too alike: the real wind fell inside the members on only about half of the days. Idea: give each member a fixed wind factor between ×0.7 and ×1.4 (spread evenly across members, mean ×1), the typical day-to-day mismatch between lake and station wind. Look for: surface coverage at longer leads, and that the band does not grow too wide (a member stays windier for the whole forecast, while the real mismatch changes within about a day). It should add to q, not replace it (earlier the wind spread explained only about 10 % of the forecast error variance).

Reproduce: Branch feat/online_error, config block online_errors.

docs.title: Ägeri check: one method, three levels
docs.text:
Status: ✅ Done · Lakes: Ägeri, 2025

Question: Ägeri is where adaptive σ ran away. Does the new method avoid it, and what do the R split and q each add?

Setup: Three runs of pn_online that differ only in the two switches (table above). Everything else as the learned R and q on Upper Lugano: memory λ = 0.95, centred forcing, gross-error check (NIS > 25), R starting at the sensor error 0.05 °C. The depth correlation of q comes from the Ägeri free run. Compared with simplified_final and the first adaptive σ run.
