Ägeri 2025, 2,503 profile times. RMSE and CRPS against the raw hourly profiler at all 239 depths; spread/RMSE and the band against the filtered profiler at the 22 assimilated depths, raw in brackets; NIS from the filter (scoring). The ported code (online_errors) reproduces both levels it was run on: R split + q 0.276 °C, R split identical up to 10 May.

Figure 10. Ägeri 2025: (left) observation error at 2, 10, 14, 18 and 30 m: the first adaptive σ (rebuilt from its saved misses), all to R, R split without and with q, and the fixed σ of simplified_final; (right) RMSE by depth against the filtered profiler, over all 2025 profile times and all profiler depths, with each run's RMSE over the whole profile (raw values in the table above).

Result: Figure 10 shows three steps.

  • All to R no longer runs away. With the new settings it is as accurate as simplified_final (0.301 against 0.299 °C), against 0.398 for the first version. Which setting stopped it (centred forcing, the gross-error check, the memory, or the start at 0.05 °C) is not separated. The mechanism is still visible, only weaker and later: at 14 m R climbs to 0.9 °C in November, against 0.24 °C for the fixed σ (the first version climbed earlier and higher).
  • The split keeps R physical. R stays at or below about 0.45 °C at every depth and the thermocline bulge disappears (RMSE 0.290). But without q nothing carries the misses it takes out of R: the filter is over-confident (NIS 1.76, the band holds 82 %).
  • q gives the main gain. RMSE 0.301 → 0.275 °C and CRPS 0.131 → 0.100, lowest at 165 of the 239 depths and within 0.01 °C of the best at 228 (12–14 m: 0.43–0.54 → 0.38–0.51 °C), and the spread rises from a fifth to three quarters of the error. With NIS 0.67 it is now somewhat cautious.

Verdict: The same story as on Upper Lugano. Use the split: R then stays physical whatever the model does. Add q whenever the spread matters, which is always for a forecast band; without it the filter is over-confident. The old failure is the reason for the split, but on Ägeri the new settings had already removed most of it.

Reproduce: Branch feat/online_error, config block online_errors.

docs.title: Model spread and structure
docs.text: The problems above all point to an under-dispersed ensemble (Open problems). These experiments look at the model side.

docs.title: Vertical localization
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: all seven (radii); example Greifensee

Question: Do the failures in the deeper layers come from spurious correlations? With 20 members, a small correlation is potentially indistinguishable from sampling noise, and without a limiting mechanism the filter acts on it anyway. Besides, observations often stop well before the lake floor, and stratification complicates the profiles. Localization forces small correlations to zero instead of trusting them.

Figure 11. Localization taper: correlation weight by state depth and observation depth.

Setup: Radii are derived offline, per lake, from a free ensemble (perturbed forcing, no analysis) in the stratified season: the ensemble anomalies (each member minus the ensemble mean) are correlated between depths, pooled over all members and times, and the radius at a given depth is the smallest separation at which that correlation first drops below a threshold of 0.45. That is 2/√20, the level below which a correlation estimated from 20 members cannot be told apart from sampling noise (two-sided 5 %): links weaker than this are ones our 20-member filter would mostly act on by chance. The radius is then used as the support of a smooth taper (Figure 11) (weight 1 at zero separation, falling to 0 at the radius). Two matrices built from the taper modify the Kalman gain. The radii come out narrow near the surface, where the gradient is sharp, and wider with depth, where the column is more coherent. Conceptually, corrections from far-away cells shrink, less spread is removed in general, and the extra spread gives a larger gain on the links that remain. Implementation details are in Localization implementation.

Figure 12. Greifensee, August 2025: error profile without localization (left) and with it (right).

Result: On Greifensee in August for example, localization brings the pooled error from 1.32 to 0.93 °C (Figure 12, left) instead of 0.97 °C (right), and trims the worst analysis error at 7.1 m from 1.76 to 1.57 °C. But the band between about 6 and 14 m is still worse than the free run in both cases. The improvements, when present, remain small.

Verdict: Long-range spurious correlations don't seem to be a central problem in our lakes in the current set up. We provide localization as an optional element rather than part of the operational configuration.

Next step: The scheme is measured per lake and ready to be tested and integrated where that stops being true: with more spread at depth, or in 3D, where spurious horizontal correlations are a bigger concern (3D).

Reproduce: feat/da-combi: src/assimilator/localization.py, notebooks/localization.py.

docs.title: Localization implementation
docs.text:
Radii are derived offline per lake from a free ensemble run in the stratified season (notebooks/localization.py): member anomalies are correlated between model depths, pooled over (member, time), and the radius at a depth is the smallest separation at which that correlation first drops below the threshold (0.45 = 2/√20, the sampling floor of a 20-member ensemble). The stratified radius is used all year: in a mixed column it localizes harder than needed, which discards some real information but never lets a spurious correlation through. That radius is the support of a Gaspari–Cohn taper: weight 1 at zero separation, falling smoothly to exactly 0 at the radius. Two matrices are built from it: a (state, obs) taper for PHᵀ and an (obs, obs) taper for HPHᵀ.

Both sides must be tapered, not just PHᵀ: The tempting shortcut is to taper only the cross-covariance, since that is the term that spreads the correction. But the gain also contains (HPHᵀ + R)⁻¹, and if that inverse is still built for the full observation set, the two halves of the gain disagree about which observations exist.

The taper must not be a boxcar: A binary on/off mask can produce a correlation structure that is no longer positive semi-definite: negative eigenvalues, and a covariance matrix that is mathematically invalid.

The taper accepts two arbitrary depth axes; per-depth radii are interpolated from the table and held flat past the table's ends rather than extrapolated; and the support of a pair is the mean of the two radii, which is what keeps ρ symmetric. Deleting localization/<lake>.json is the kill switch; the scheme falls back to a flat 5 m radius.

The intended consequence is that nothing far below the deepest observation gets updated. The deep water free-runs, and that is correct behaviour rather than a limitation: there is no information down there, so the model should be trusted rather than nudged by noise.

docs.title: Parameter sensitivity
docs.text:
Status: 🔬 Open · Lakes: Upper Lugano

Question: An obvious source of additional spread is the model itself. Three clear candidates, all already used in Simstrat's own calibration: f_wind (wind factor: wind speed is multiplied by it), p_lw (longwave radiation factor: longwave irradiance is multiplied by it) and a_seiche (seiche factor: how much wind energy is absorbed by internal waves). How much spread could they give, and where?

Setup: Seven continuous free runs over 2025, identical unperturbed forcing and identical warm start: control plus a low/high pair per parameter (f_wind ±10 %, p_lw ±3 %, a_seiche ×3 / ÷3, all inside the lake-calibrator bounds). Shown with the control subtracted, at 1, 11 and 30 m, against raw hourly observations. Light grey is the free ensemble from forcing perturbation; darker grey the assimilated one.

Figure 13. Parameter sensitivity envelopes at 1, 11 and 30 m, Upper Lugano 2025, control subtracted, against raw hourly observations; light grey: free forcing ensemble, darker grey: assimilated ensemble.

Result: In Figure 13, at 1 m, the error to explain reaches −2 °C in midsummer. The AR(1) forcing ensemble is about ±0.3 °C. The parameter envelopes reach 0.5–1.2 °C. At 11 m, observations minus free run peaks near +3 °C in September. The forcing spread is still around ±0.3 °C, but a_seiche and f_wind open to about ±1 °C, and they open in the stratified season, which is exactly where more spread would be particularly helpful. At 30 m the error is smaller, but more spread would still help.

Verdict: Parameter variability could be a viable way to insert uncertainty into the deep column. Two ways to use it follow: perturbing the parameters, or estimating them.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; easily reproducible, scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Parameter perturbation
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: Upper Lugano

Question: Parameter differences are structural, so the analysis should have a harder time collapsing them, and it moves uncertainty away from the observation error and toward the model, where it partly belongs: more model spread means the observations are trusted more. Does it help the filter?

Setup: Seven assimilation experiments, native EnKF (seasonal σ). The only thing that changes is which model parameter is spread across the members, and by how much. Members are spread deterministically around the calibrated value, and the control member keeps it.

perturbation mean spread (°C) spread below 19 m pooled NIS RMSE, hourly none (operational) 0.072 0.033 0.55 −26.3 % a_seiche_w ×/÷ 5 0.072 0.033 0.55 −26.3 % f_wind ±10 % 0.074 0.034 0.54 −26.5 % a_seiche ×/÷ 5 0.082 0.039 0.55 −26.1 % p_lw ±5 % + a_seiche ±80 % 0.084 0.036 0.50 −27.3 % p_lw ±10 % 0.090 0.035 0.49 −27.4 % f_wind ±50 % 0.108 0.052 0.48 −27.3 % p_lw ±25 % 0.116 0.037 0.44 −28.3 %

Result: It works in the direction predicted, but it is small. More parameter spread gives a slightly better analysis. The best case, p_lw ±25 %, moves RMSE from −26.3 % to −28.3 %, and it cuts the total depth-months made worse by assimilation from 41 to 25 out of 192. The corrections become bigger (median 0.013 → 0.017 °C at the surface), which is what a filter with a wider ensemble is supposed to do.

The amplitudes in parameter perturbations that achieve this are not defensible. p_lw ±25 % is an eightfold exaggeration of the ±3 % used in the sensitivity test, and the calibrated values across our seven lakes span less. The perturbations we can eventually justify (f_wind ±10 %, a_seiche ×/÷ 5) change essentially nothing: 0.072 → 0.074 and 0.082 °C of spread. σ still dominates and the imbalance grows with depth.

Figure 14. Upper Lugano 2025: ensemble spread (solid) vs actual error (dashed) and σ (grey), daily and 3-day assimilation, with and without p_lw ±10 %.

Where it becomes interesting is at lower frequency: In Figure 14, solid lines are ensemble spread, dashed the actual error it should cover, grey σ. With p_lw ±10 %, the spread grows by about a quarter at daily frequency, and by more than a third when assimilating every 3 days, because the parameter differences have longer to act between analyses. At 3 days this is enough to bring the accuracy back to almost exactly the daily result, while assimilating a third of the profiles.

Verdict: Not adopted at defensible amplitudes; only worth it at lower assimilation frequencies.

Next step: The 3-day result is a quick test only: the deepest measurement actually got worse, so the way the additional spread is generated needs more care, but it is a promising direction.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Joint state–parameter estimation
docs.text:
Status: 🔬 Open · Lakes: Upper Lugano

Question: Instead of fixing the parameter spread, can the filter estimate the parameters together with the temperature? There is precedent in the literature (e.g. the FLARE framework of Thomas et al. (2020)).

Setup: The filter updates f_wind, p_lw and a_seiche at every analysis. At the start each of the 20 members draws its own set of values around the calibrated ones: p_lw with a 5 % spread in logit space, bounded to 0.8–1.2; a_seiche and f_wind in log space, with a spread of ×1.65 and about 10 %. The transforms keep the parameters positive and within bounds, and the draws are stratified and shuffled so the three parameters start uncorrelated. The transformed parameters are appended to each member's temperature profile as an extended state. Since they are not observed, they change only through their ensemble covariance with the observed temperatures, and the temperature update itself is unchanged. Between analyses they stay fixed. Each update narrows their spread; a floor holds the spread from collapsing.

Figure 15. Joint state–parameter estimation, Upper Lugano 2025: the members' values of the three parameters, coloured by month; the star marks the calibrated values.

Result: The cloud in Figure 15 shows the members' values through 2025, coloured by month; the star marks the calibrated values. They do not converge. They keep moving with the seasons, with much less wind and much more seiche mixing in summer, and the longwave factor pinned to its lower bound. The filter is using the parameters to absorb the seasonal bias. The accuracy ends up the same as without updating them, but reached in a different way.

Verdict: That opens real questions. Can a parameter be updated daily? Is 20 members enough for a joint state? Do the parameters stay physically defensible (broad bounds help, but probably something tighter is needed)? And there is an underlying attribution problem: we change the model's physics and its state at the same time on limited evidence, so the parameters can absorb errors that aren't theirs, and they trade off against each other.

Next step: A single run both corrects the temperatures and yields a distribution of the parameters, which could be a cheap first estimate to compare against a traditional calibration or to analyse potential systematic model failures. Coming back to the spread question, the next step would be adding justified random variability to the model state itself: structural uncertainty through state perturbation (see Uncertainty band).

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Deep mixing
docs.text:
Status: 🔬 Open · Lakes: Lake Lugano, 1987–2025

Question: Can assimilation improve the representation of deep mixing in Simstrat?

Setup: The buoy stops at 40 m, but for Lake Lugano there are almost 40 years of CTD casts, one every two weeks, down to 280 m, and we started by assimilating those. The profiles were thinned to a coarser grid as described in Method; the seiche filtering is not possible on fortnightly casts.

Figure 16. Lake Lugano, 1987–2025: model − observation, free run vs CTD assimilation; arrows mark the winters the lake mixed below 100 m.

Result: The free run starts too cold in the deep water and slowly builds up a warm bias. It mixes all the way below 100 m in 10 winters, while the lake did so in only two (the arrows in Figure 16). With assimilation the deep temperatures are corrected: RMSE between 30 and 100 m almost halves, 0.29 → 0.16 °C, and at 1 m it drops from 0.88 to 0.79 °C.

Figure 17. Independent check of the CTD-assimilated run against the 2025 Upper Lugano buoy.

Against the 2025 buoy, which this run never saw, the error still drops from 0.83 to 0.72 °C. But look at the dotted lines in Figure 17: deep mixing becomes more frequent, 15 winters instead of 10.

Verdict: For now, assimilating temperature fixes the temperature but tends to make the mixing worse. Correcting the state may change when and how deep the model overturns.

A later finding may explain part of this: the forcing perturbation makes every member windier than the control (Centred forcing perturbations), and more wind brings more mixing. The Lugano run above was made before this was found, with uncentred forcing. On Geneva, with centred forcing, the free run and the assimilated run mix to the bottom in the same winters (both still too often), but Geneva has not been run without centring, so the comparison is indirect. The Lugano run has not yet been repeated with centred forcing.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: The same layout in 3D
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: Lake Lugano (Delft3D-FLOW), one-month test window

Question: Does the ensemble DA layout transfer to a 3D model, so that it can sit beside Simstrat in the module as an optional engine?

Setup: Delft3D-FLOW on Lake Lugano, driven the same way: OpenDA treats the model as a black box, writes a restart file, launches the model in a container, reads the output, adjusts the restart, and repeats, so the simulation advances window by window. The model is expensive, so these experiments use 7 members instead of 20. A big new thing in 3D is that the covariance also spreads a single station's correction horizontally to nearby cells, so one buoy can inform a whole region. That is attractive, because we have few stations, and risky at the same time: with seven members, spurious horizontal correlations become a real concern, more so than in 1D.

Figure 18. Delft3D-FLOW, Lake Lugano: satellite surface temperature (left) and cells where the assimilated run is closer to it than the operational run (right, green).

Result: Surface-only assimilation of the five stations around Lake Lugano gives promising first results: against a satellite surface-temperature snapshot (Figure 18, left), the assimilated run is closer than the operational Alplakes run in 94 % of the cells (right, green).

Next step: The first results point clearly at the need for a vertical localization mechanism, or for deep measurements where they exist. Beyond that, it opens up possibilities to explore also assimilating the satellite surface temperature itself, providing the whole lake surface, but at lower resolution.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Recent work
docs.text: Work started after the results above. Numbers are preliminary, and the runs are not part of the operational setup.

docs.title: Does assimilation disturb the model's natural variability?
docs.text:
Status: ✅ Passes · Lakes: Upper Lugano, 2025

Question: A daily correction is a jump in the model state. Does it leave the model's own oscillations intact, or does it add artificial ones?

Setup: The operational setup (simplified_final: 20 members, one analysis a day at 06 UTC) against the free run, over 2025. Power spectra of the hourly temperature at every depth (one FFT over the year) for the free run, the ensemble mean with assimilation, and the buoy observations (the raw 10-minute record averaged to hourly, not filtered, so that the variability being compared is still in it); plus the mean absolute hourly temperature change by hour of day.

Figure 19. Upper Lugano 2025, simplified_final: spectral energy of hourly temperature by depth and period, without and with DA and their ratio (top); spectra at 0.5, 11 and 40 m with the observations (middle); spectra of the model − observation error (bottom).

Result so far: The assimilated run keeps generally the spectral shape of the free run at every depth (Figure 19), so the model's natural behaviour is preserved. At short periods (days to hours) and at 11 and 40 m, the energy with assimilation lies between the free run and the observations: it moves towards the real lake, which has far more short-period energy than the 1D model.

Figure 20. Upper Lugano 2025, simplified_final: mean absolute hourly temperature change by hour of day at 0.5, 11 and 40 m, without and with DA; the update falls in the 06 → 07 UTC step.

Each update is a single step (Figure 20, the 06 → 07 UTC hour), with no oscillation after it; in every other hour the assimilated run changes like the free run.

Next step: Results support the claim in Overview that the shocks are not generating artificial oscillations and that the scheme is safe to run unattended.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Oxygen assimilation
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: Ägeri (Nov 2022 – Jun 2026), Murten (Jun 2022 – Jun 2026)

Question: Can the same filter correct dissolved oxygen as well as temperature, and what does the vertical coverage of the oxygen data change?

Setup: Temperature and oxygen are assimilated together, with their updates decoupled (temperature observations correct only temperature, oxygen only oxygen), a seasonal σ for oxygen, and a small white noise (standard deviation 2 mmol/m³) on every member's oxygen after each analysis, to widen an oxygen spread that was far below its innovations. Here the profilers are assimilated and the CTD casts are only used for scoring; the next two experiments change which data go in:

Data Ägeri Murten Profiler, temperature 23 depths, 2–79 m 35 depths, 0.5–43 m Profiler, oxygen 23 depths, 2–79 m 3 depths: 25, 40 and 41 m Profiler period, as assimilated Nov 2022 – Oct 2026, seiche-filtered, one profile a day at 23 UTC Jun 2022 – Jul 2026 (oxygen from Dec 2022), seiche-filtered, one profile a day at 04 UTC CTD casts (T and O₂) 14 casts, about quarterly, Dec 2022 – Mar 2026, 0.5–78.5 m 42 casts, about monthly, Jul 2022 – Dec 2025, 0.5–42.5 m Oxygen assimilation profiler in, casts for scoring profiler in, casts for scoring Depth thinning 5 of the 23 profiler depths in, all profiler depths and casts for scoring – CTD interpolation casts in, profiler for scoring casts in, profiler for scoring

Ägeri's profiler is high-resolution both in time and in depth; Murten's is high-resolution in time, but measures oxygen only in the deep water.

Figure 21. Ägeri, Nov 2022 – Jun 2026, profiler assimilated: RMSE profiles of T and O₂, free run vs EnKF, against the profiler (top) and the CTD casts (bottom).

Result so far.

  • Ägeri: large improvement (Figure 21): O₂ error against the profiler drops by about 45 % (46 → 25 mmol/m³), and is spread more evenly over the column, with large gains at 10–20 m and again in the deep water, but not directly at the lake bed. Temperature 0.52 → 0.32 °C.
  • Murten: smaller improvement (Figure 22): O₂ drops by about 18 % against the CTD casts (69 → 57 mmol/m³), mostly at the deeper levels near the three oxygen sensors. Temperature 0.79 → 0.45 °C against the profiler.

Figure 22. Murten, Jun 2022 – Jun 2026, profiler assimilated: RMSE profiles of T and O₂, free run vs EnKF, against the profiler (top) and the CTD casts (bottom).

Figure 23. Ägeri, 31 October 2024: O₂ profile, observations (red), free run (dashed) and EnKF (blue).

The filter struggles right above the lake bed. In the example of Figure 23 the assimilated profile (blue) fits the observations (red) as well as it can, but keeps the wrong shape at the bottom. This points to a structural model error: the model cannot simulate the oxygen depletion at the bottom boundary.

Verdict so far: Vertical coverage matters, and the bottom boundary has to be fixed in the model, not by assimilation.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Observation depth thinning
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: Ägeri

Question: How many depths do we need for a useful improvement? If the filter can interpolate vertically, fewer sensors could be enough in the field.

Setup: Same Ägeri profiler data as above, temperature and oxygen, but keep only 5 of the 23 depths (2, 10, 20, 40, 70 m; a second layout 2, 7, 15, 45, 70 m) and score against all profiler depths and hours, with the 23-depth run as reference.

Figure 24. Ägeri: RMSE profiles with 5 assimilated depths (blue) vs 23 (dashed) vs free run; red fill where 5 depths are worse than the free run.

Result so far: With 5 depths, about 35–40 % of the temperature gain (0.52 → 0.45 °C, against 0.32 with 23 depths) and about 70 % of the oxygen gain (46 → 31 mmol/m³, against 25) remain. These are scored on the profiler, of which the 5-depth run assimilates a few depths; against the CTD casts, which neither run assimilates, the shares are almost the same (about 40 % for temperature, 0.43 → 0.35 °C against 0.24; about 70 % for oxygen, 47 → 34 mmol/m³ against 28). The deep levels above the bottom keep good gains with just a few measurements; the rest to a lower extent. Each layout opens possible new gaps between its sensors (red areas in Figure 24, where the filter is worse than the free run) and the oxygen and temperature structure of each lake needs to carefully be taken into account and requires more study.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: CTD casts as a temporal interpolator
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: Ägeri, Murten

Question: Many lakes have only monthly or quarterly CTD casts. With only those assimilated, does the run give realistic profiles between the casts?

Setup: Assimilate the CTD casts (T and O₂) instead of the profiler: 14 casts on Ägeri, 42 on Murten (see the data table); the high-resolution profiler, never seen by the filter, becomes an independent check of the interpolation in time. Note the rows in Figures 25 and 26 are swapped with respect to the profiler runs: top row = independent profiler, bottom row = the assimilated casts, one hour after the analysis.

Figure 25. Ägeri, CTD casts assimilated: RMSE profiles against the independent profiler (top) and the casts, one hour after the analysis (bottom).

Result so far:

  • Ägeri: it works essentially only in the deep water: Between casts, O₂ at 50–80 m stays closer to the profiler than the free run; above about 40 m it is no better than the free run. Overall about −10 % (O₂ 46 → 41 mmol/m³, T 0.52 → 0.48 °C), not evenly distributed.
  • Murten: similar (Figure 26). Gains where observations are available (O₂ 62 → 53 mmol/m³, T 0.79 → 0.65 °C). Here we would have expected oxygen gains up to about 15 m.

Figure 26. Murten, CTD casts assimilated: RMSE profiles against the independent profiler (top) and the casts, one hour after the analysis (bottom).

These runs need the forcing ensemble centred on the original forcing, because the observations are weeks apart (Centred forcing perturbations).

Verdict so far: Assimilation is a promising temporal interpolator for the deep layers, but not for the faster-varying upper layers with monthly or sub-monthly sampling.

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Centred forcing perturbations
docs.text:
Status: (✅) Positive, potentially to be adopted · Lakes: Ägeri, Murten, Geneva

Question: Does the forcing perturbation shift the ensemble mean away from the original forcing, and does that matter?

Setup: The AR(1) noise is added to the wind components U and V with zero mean. But the wind speed is the length of the vector, so noise in either direction makes it larger on average. With the option center_perturbations, each forcing row is rescaled so that the ensemble-mean wind speed, solar radiation and air temperature equal the unperturbed forcing.

Result so far: Without centring, every member is windier than the control: the ensemble-mean wind speed is 63 % above it on Ägeri (2.52 against 1.55 m/s), 57 % on Geneva and 31 % on Murten. With centring, the two agree to within about 2 %. With daily assimilation the filter corrects the resulting bias every day, but when the observations are weeks apart (CTD casts) it accumulates between casts: more wind, more mixing, a deeper overturn. That may explain part of the more frequent deep mixing seen on Lake Lugano (Deep mixing).

Next step: The operational setup (simplified_final) runs without centring, so check its effect there too, and repeat the Lugano deep-mixing run with centred forcing.

Reproduce: Branch feat/online_error, option center_perturbations.

docs.title: Long-term CTD assimilation in Geneva
docs.text:
Status: 🔬 Open · Lakes: Geneva (LéXPLORE casts, Nov 2019 – Jun 2026)

In short

  • The casts correct both variables well. Temperature RMSE against the profiler 1.19 → 0.87 °C; oxygen RMSE at the casts 105 → 38 mmol/m³.
  • Winter remains wrong, and neither tuning knob fixes it. More forcing noise or a smaller winter σ leave the errors unchanged: the model mixes too deep in winter, in every member alike.

Question: Can six and a half years of CTD casts correct temperature and oxygen together, and does the result hold against the high-resolution profiler, which is not assimilated?

Main result (annual σ 0.297 °C):

RMSE Free run EnKF Temperature, against the profiler 1.19 °C 0.87 °C Oxygen, at the casts 105 mmol/m³ 38 mmol/m³
  • Oxygen: the free run's deep water is about 120 mmol/m³ too low below 40 m. The filter needs about a year to lift it (NIS/n about 20 at the start, about 1 from 2022 to 2025).
  • The ensemble is far too narrow: spread 0.026 °C against σ 0.297 °C, so all the uncertainty sits in σ.

Two attempts to improve winter, neither helped:

  1. Perturb air temperature too (AR(1), sd 1.67 °C): the winter spread stays around 0.03 °C, because the deep mixed layer damps the noise.
  2. A smaller winter σ (0.10 °C from November to April, the scatter of same-day double casts):
    • Too small: winter NIS/n (December–March) goes from 0.73 to 4.95. The double-cast scatter measures the casts, not what the model cannot represent; the innovations point to about 0.25 °C, close to the annual value.
    • No accuracy gain: temperature RMSE is unchanged (0.864 against 0.865 °C), oxygen RMSE 38 → 40 mmol/m³, and the winter mixed layer stays about 15 m too deep (error about 22 m).
    • Why: the stronger updates halve the already tiny spread (0.028 → 0.014 °C), and the model drifts back between casts, so each cast meets the same misfit.

Deep mixing, year by year: The casts mix to the station bottom (about 100 m) only in 2020, 2021 and 2026. The model reaches the bottom almost every winter, with or without assimilation; in 2022 and 2024 the lake stopped at about 65 m and 45 m. Unlike on Lake Lugano, assimilation does not make deep mixing more frequent: over the full 309 m column the free run overturns completely in 2021 and 2022, the EnKF only in 2022.

Verdict so far: The remaining error is a systematic winter model error (mixing too deep, surface too cold, the same in every member), not a filter-tuning problem (Open problems).

Next step: Most of the 0.25 °C winter σ is model uncertainty that the ensemble does not carry. A process noise on the temperature profile, as in the learned R and q, would move it into the ensemble, so σ could shrink towards the cast scatter and each cast would correct more. In a near-isothermal winter column the noise must not create inversions (the profile constraint discussed there).

Reproduce: Not in the repository; scripts available from the author on request.

docs.title: Method
docs.text:
Last updated: November 2026.

In short

A 20-member ensemble is made by adding AR(1) noise to wind and solar radiation. Once a day, at a per-lake night hour, a stochastic EnKF corrects the temperature profile of every member. The observations are filtered below 4 m to remove internal-seiche motion the 1D model cannot reproduce, and thinned to a per-lake depth grid. Their uncertainty σ is a representativeness error, not instrument error: one value per lake and season.

docs.title: The filters
docs.text:
The Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) updates the state by weighing two uncertainties against each other: how wrong the ensemble thinks the model is, and how wrong we say the observation is. The Kalman gain can be read as a trust ratio: if the ensemble is confident, the observation moves the state very little; if the ensemble is uncertain, the observation wins and pulls the state a lot. The property that makes this filter attractive for a lake column is that information propagates in depth through the ensemble covariance, which comes from the model spread and so reflects the model physics: an observation at one depth can correct the whole profile, by an amount the ensemble says those depths move together (and, in a 3D model, this also translates to whole regions of the lake). We use the stochastic EnKF: where each member is updated with its own perturbed observation, to avoid ensemble collapse.

The Particle Filter (PF), on the other hand, never builds a correction. It re-weights and clones whole member states in proportion to their likelihood, so every surviving trajectory stays a physically untouched Simstrat run. The price is that the analysis can only ever contain states the model itself produced: if no member happens to have the right profile, there is no mechanism to produce a fitting one and potentially would need more spread (ensemble members) or more effort in creating varying particles (parameter sampling).

The native engine also has a cheaper best-member selection, which clones the best-fitting member onto all the others as a simple reference (details).

Why an ensemble filter and not a standard Kalman filter? The models are nonlinear, which a classic KF handles poorly. An ensemble method treats the model as a black box, so the same strategy transfers to other models well (see 3D); it needs no derivatives to build the error covariances; and the members run naturally in parallel.

Decision: the EnKF is the operational filter

  • Alternatives: particle filter (OpenDA), best-member selection (native).
  • Evidence: the EnKF wins on every lake, on both engines; selection is worse than no assimilation on three lakes (Results).
  • Revisit if: the ensemble becomes much larger, or the spread at depth grows enough that members genuinely differ there too; that is where the PF fails now.

docs.title: Where the spread comes from
docs.text:
You cannot run an ensemble filter without spread, and the spread has to come from a defensible source. We generate it by perturbing the meteorological forcing, a major and well-known uncertainty factor for lake models. This forcing perturbation is the only component that generates spread in the module right now.

Figure 1. Ensemble envelope (blue) around the control station forcing (black), one wind component, Lake Lugano, July 2025.

Figure 1 shows a blue ensemble envelope around the black control station forcing, here for one wind component on Lake Lugano during July 2025.

Only three variables are perturbed: wind U, wind V, solar radiation. Temperature, vapour pressure, cloud cover and rain pass through untouched. Those three dominate the surface momentum and energy budget, and restricting to them keeps the mechanism simpler and potentially more interpretable.

Each member gets one AR(1) noise series added to the control forcing, so that the perturbation carries part of the temporal correlation of real forcing errors:

xₜ = φ·xₜ₋₁ + σ·εₜ ,      ε ~ N(0,1)

We assume that the amplitude of the perturbation represents the mismatch between the lake's reference meteorological station and the average conditions over the lake, and measure it as the standard deviation of the ICON reanalysis averaged over the lake minus the control forcing, s = std(ICON − control). The persistence φ = exp(−1/τ) cannot be measured precisely: we bracket it between two proxies, the autocorrelation of the residual series and of the station signal itself, and take the end that gives more persistence, hence potentially more spread, which benefits the EnKF. The size of one hourly kick then follows as σ = s·√(1−φ²). The full calibration is in Perturbation calibration.

The practical advantage is that the ensemble is generated at the forcing, not at the state. Members diverge the way the weather diverges, and each one remains a physically consistent Simstrat run. This is done to keep the filter from shocking the model when it injects a correction.

Decision: spread from forcing perturbation only

  • Alternatives: parameter perturbation, joint state–parameter estimation, state perturbation (Experiments); not tested, driving each member with a member of an NWP ensemble (COSMO-E), as Safin et al. (2022) do for Lake Geneva, which keeps the physical correlations between variables without a statistical noise model.
  • Evidence: keeps every member a physically consistent run and the corrections small; the defensible parameter perturbations added only little spread.
  • Revisit if: a defensible source of spread at depth is found, e.g. the process noise of the forecast uncertainty band, or parameter spread at longer analysis intervals (Parameter perturbation); under-dispersion is the main open problem (Open problems). The forcing ensemble is also not centred yet (Open problems).

docs.title: When to assimilate
docs.text:
Figure 2. Choosing the assimilation hour. Left: bias and random error of the free run by hour of day, Lake Geneva. Right: RMSE by assimilation frequency, Upper Lugano 2025.

The left panel of Figure 2 shows how the bias and random error are distributed over the day for Lake Geneva. The right one shows how the accuracy of the assimilation decreases with decreasing frequency for Lake Lugano.

Daily: A daily frequency reduces the error correlation between successive analyses, and avoids a sub-daily reversal of the error sign eating into the potential gains. Assimilating more often would make the filter less efficient (information counted twice) and noisier (potential reversals of the corrections). Going below daily costs accuracy (Assimilation frequency). This agrees with Wander et al. (2024), who found daily assimilation the most skilful for a 1-day forecast, but weekly assimilation the most skilful for 8–35-day horizons.

At a specific hour: Using a free run, we take the mean and standard deviation of the model–observation error over the days, hour by hour. Among the hours the lake samples on at least 30 days, we keep those whose bias is at most 0.2 times their day-to-day scatter, and take the one with the largest scatter: the most correctable error for little injected bias. The reasoning: the deterministic part of the gap is potentially a correction for something the model's physics might undo.

Only the surface layer, above 4 m, enters this choice. That is where the diurnal cycle lives, and so where the hour makes a bigger difference. Below 4 m the observations go through the seiche filter, whose trailing window (11 h or more, depending on the lake) smooths most of the diurnal signal out: there the hour matters much less.

By this measure noon, the hour used by the current BETA, turns out to be a bad choice. The exact rule is in the Tutorial.

At night: Candidates are restricted to 23–06 UTC, so that every lake is sampled at a comparable point in its diurnal cycle, with the operational bonus that it is off-hours. This is the window behind the results here; the code's default is now 00–06 UTC, and assimilate.py fit hour --window 23-6 reproduces these hours.

Only hours the lake actually samples are candidates, with adaptation where a fixed frequency cannot be guaranteed (Greifensee takes the first reading between 00 and 06 UTC each day). Days without a profile in the window are skipped. The hour picked for each lake is in the per-lake card.

Decision: daily, at a per-lake night hour

  • Alternatives: every 3 or 7 days; noon (the BETA); any hour of the day.
  • Evidence: daily beats 3- and 7-day on Upper Lugano (Assimilation frequency); noon maximises injected bias.
  • Revisit if: more model spread makes lower frequencies competitive (with p_lw ±10 %, assimilating every 3 days already matches the daily accuracy: Parameter perturbation), or a lake's sampling schedule changes.

docs.title: The raw signal at depth is not the signal we can use
docs.text:
Figure 3. Raw temperature at 11 m against the model, Upper Lugano, 25 June to 5 July 2025.

Figure 3 shows a raw temperature observation at 11 m depth, 25 June to 5 July 2025, Upper Lake Lugano. The sensor swings by up to 10 °C within a few hours. The dashed line is what Simstrat predicts at the same times, and it is nearly flat, with only an underlying trend visible. (The series is debiased here to make the contrast more visible.)

The cause is internal wave motion: the steep thermal gradient is displaced vertically past a fixed instrument. The sensor is right and the signal is real.

But a 1D model cannot reproduce it by construction. There is no horizontal dimension for an internal wave to propagate in. So this variability, which can exceed the entire actual model–observation discrepancy we are trying to correct, is not an error the filter should try to fix. Feeding these thermocline-displacement excursions to the filter would continuously drag the whole column toward an unstable state that the model cannot maintain.

docs.title: Filtering the observations causally
docs.text:
Figure 4. Causal filtering of the observations at 11 m, Upper Lugano: hourly series (black) and filtered series (blue).

Figure 4 shows the original time series of the temperature at 11 m in Upper Lugano in black (already aggregated to hourly) and, in blue, the observation filtered with a 27.3 h trailing window set by the seiche period. The fix is to remove large part of the signal the model cannot represent. Three constraints shape the solution:

  • It must be causal: no leakage of future information, because this runs operationally (a centred moving average would be better but not usable). We use a trailing moving average.
  • It must be split in depth: above a threshold (currently 4 m) the series passes through untouched. Surface temperature does not suffer thermocline displacement in the same way, and we do not want to blur an important fast signal.
  • It must be set physically, per lake: the trailing window comes from a two-layer approximation, using the lake length and its stratification at peak, giving a characteristic fundamental internal-seiche period for each basin (per-lake card).

Residual variability at depth drops from around 10 °C to roughly 1–1.5 °C. Still not small, but far more digestible for the filter. What the filtering gains is shown in Observation filtering.

docs.title: Too many sensors
docs.text:
Figure 5. Thinning a dense sensor chain to the target depth grid.

Profilers and moorings differ in vertical and temporal resolution, and a filter that ingests whatever it is handed behaves differently on each. Some instruments, such as those on Ägeri and Greifensee, report at sub-metre resolution (Figure 5: 160 depths at 0.1 m). Neighbouring sensors at that spacing are near-copies: two thermistors 10–25 cm apart in a well-mixed layer report the same water, and their error is essentially one error, not two independent ones. The filter counts them as independent evidence and can grow over-confident, pull too hard toward the observations and shrink the posterior spread. With only 20 members, ensemble collapse is something we want to avoid as much as possible.

The solution is a per-lake target vertical grid: dense profiles are thinned to a manageable resolution (here 17 assimilated depths), preferring the depths with fewer gaps. That also makes the seven lakes more comparable with each other. The large observation uncertainty defined below further counteracts the residual over-confidence.

docs.title: σ is not instrument error
docs.text:
The unrepresented variability is still present in smaller magnitude at filtered depths but also at unfiltered depths, and this mismatch cannot easily be covered by spread generated through forcing perturbation alone: we are asking the ensemble to cover variability that no member could produce with the current setup.

The sensors are generally very accurate; their precision is not the issue. So the uncertainty we hand the filter has to come from somewhere else, or the filter will pull far too hard toward the observations. We therefore define σ not as instrument error but as representativeness error: an honest statement of what the model cannot reproduce and is currently assigned as observation error. It varies by lake, by depth, and by season. That is partly process: variability, like the internal-wave signal above, that a 1D column cannot reproduce. And it is partly space: a buoy measures one point, while Simstrat represents a horizontally averaged column for the whole lake.

docs.title: A simple operational recipe
docs.text:
For the operational setup we make three deliberate simplifying assumptions: the observation uncertainty is fixed in depth, seasonal (mixed vs stratified), and comparable from year to year.

The recipe: take the gap between a free run and the filtered observations at the assimilation times over a reference year (for the results presented here, 2025 for data availability over an entire year for all lakes). Split the series into seasons and remove each season's own mean (that is bias, not random uncertainty). Take the standard deviation of what remains as a variability proxy, and aggregate with the median across depths. This is deliberately a simple approach aimed at being a justified and generalizable approach to start running the multiple lakes operationally.

season upperlugano maggiore greifensee geneva aegeri hallwil murten mixed 0.30 0.70 0.52 0.28 0.24 0.41 0.34 stratified 0.59 1.17 0.94 0.59 0.24 0.39 0.60

The stratified season generally wants a larger σ, exactly what you expect if the dominant error source is thermocline displacement. Two lakes break the pattern: Ägeri, which we restrict to a single scalar because the seasonal split performed worse, and Hallwil, whose mixed season is marginally larger than its stratified one and represents an odd case.

σ here is the honest statement of what the model cannot reproduce. The uncomfortable part is that it still occupies essentially the whole uncertainty budget (the ensemble remains too narrow and model uncertainty underrepresented).

docs.title: Why the seasonal σ stays operational, for now
docs.text:
We tested three alternatives: σ resolved in depth, rescaled against the filter's own innovations, and estimated on the fly from the innovations (Experiments). Each calibrates better than the seasonal σ. None of them is clearly more accurate. For an unattended system, three things tip the balance.

Simple. The seasonal σ is two numbers per lake, fitted once and written in the config. Anyone can read them, both engines use them unchanged, and the filter's trust is known before the run starts. The adaptive σ is a moving quantity. It needs a two-week history of innovations that must survive restarts and outages.

Cautious. The approaches fail in opposite directions, and only one of those directions is safe. The seasonal σ is too large (NIS ≈ 0.6), so the filter under-trusts the observations and corrections stay generally small. The adaptive σ can fall significantly and might pull hard where it has little information about its own error. A sudden change after a quiet fortnight, whether a real event or a faulty sensor, is over-trusted until the window catches up. And because σ is estimated from innovations the filter itself shaped, errors can reinforce themselves in both directions. Good corrections shrink the innovations, which shrinks σ, so the filter pulls harder. A growing model bias enlarges them, which raises σ, so the filter lets go. On Ägeri the second loop took more than half the gain (Adaptive σ). The seasonal σ is measured against a free run the filter never touched, so it cannot enter either loop.

Differences. What do we give up? In general accuracy, nothing: the seasonal σ is as good or better on six of seven lakes, and Upper Lugano's advantage for the adaptive σ did not carry over to the other lakes. What we give up is an honest uncertainty: the seasonal filter often says it is less sure than it really is and it trusts the observations less than it could.

Decision: fixed seasonal σ per lake

  • Alternatives: depth-resolved σ, rescaled σ (Experiments); adaptive σ and the learned R and q (Learning the errors online).
  • Evidence: as accurate or better on six of seven lakes, cannot enter a feedback loop, and the choice of fitting year barely matters (Fitting year).
  • Revisit if: the ensemble spread at depth grows (σ would no longer have to fill the whole budget), the learned R and q holds on more lakes and in forecasts, or an observation file changes: σ is only valid for the file it was fitted on.

docs.title: The EnKF in full
docs.text:
Two quantities are computed from the ensemble spread:

PHᵀ  ≈  Aᶠ (HAᶠ)ᵀ / (N−1)          how the whole column co-varies with the measured depths
HPHᵀ ≈  (HAᶠ)(HAᶠ)ᵀ / (N−1)        the forecast's own spread at the observed locations

The first is the one that matters most for a 1D lake column: it is what lets an observation at 5 m adjust the temperature at 12 m, because the ensemble says those depths move together. The gain then weighs the two uncertainties,

K  =  PHᵀ (HPHᵀ + R)⁻¹

and each member is updated with its own perturbed observation,

xᵢᵃ  =  xᵢᶠ + K (dᵢ + εᵢ) ,      εᵢ ~ N(0, R)

which helps prevent ensemble collapse, i.e. the spread shrinking to nothing and the filter ceasing to listen to the observations at all.

symbol meaning N ensemble size A ensemble spread about the mean P forecast error covariance R observation error covariance K Kalman gain H observation operator X state vector (forecast / analysis) dᵢ innovation = observation − member forecast εᵢ observation perturbation drawn for member i

The structure of K explains the entire calibration effort in Results and Experiments: it is essentially model spread / (model spread + observation error). If R is too small the filter believes the observations completely and pushes the model around. If R is too large you pay for an ensemble that corrects very little and ends up reproducing a free run. There is no neutral choice; it is always a balance.

R is diagonal. Each observation gets its own variance σ² on the diagonal, and every off-diagonal term is zero: R = diag(σ²), in both engines. In other words, the observation errors are assumed independent of each other, and the σ described above is the whole of R. This is a simplification: neighbouring depths share part of their representativeness error (e.g. the same internal wave moves the whole thermocline), so their errors are in reality correlated. We keep it diagonal because those correlations are difficult to estimate reliably from the data (and estimating them wrong could do more damage than good); because the setup already compensates for them in two ways (profiles are thinned so that near-duplicate sensors are not counted twice (Too many sensors), and σ is deliberately large); and because OpenDA's standard observers, including the one we use, only take one standard deviation per observation: the OpenDA EnKF itself accepts a full R, but providing one would need a custom observer.

docs.title: The PF (OpenDA)
docs.text:
A SIR particle filter with residual resampling. Each member is weighted by the Gaussian likelihood of its own innovation,

wᵢ  ∝  exp( −½ · dᵢᵀ R⁻¹ dᵢ ) ,      w̃ᵢ = wᵢ / Σⱼ wⱼ ,      Σᵢ w̃ᵢ = 1

after which members are resampled so each is duplicated roughly in proportion to w̃ᵢ. Copies are exact clones of the full model state.

Note what does not appear: no gain, no covariance, no PHᵀ. The PF never asks how the column co-varies. It cannot use an observation at 5 m to construct a correction at 12 m; it can only prefer members that already happened to be right at both.

This is the weak point at our ensemble size. With 20 members and a state vector spanning every depth cell, the likelihood is sharply peaked: a few members can dominate, the filter can collapse to a single particle, resampling fills the ensemble with copies of one trajectory, and the spread is almost all gone until the following day's forcing perturbations rebuild it. That is the well-known dimensionality limitation of particle filters, and it is why the EnKF is the operational choice.

docs.title: The native engine's "PF" is a selection scheme
docs.text:
The native engine scores each member by a depth-weighted RMSE over the window (hourly data),

RMSEᵢ = sqrt( Σ_z w_z (xᵢ(z) − y(z))² / Σ_z w_z )

with trapezoidal layer thicknesses as weights w_z, so a tight cluster of sensors does not outvote a sparsely instrumented part of the column. The filter then clones the best member onto all the others. In the language above, that is a particle filter whose weights have been replaced by a hard argmin:

w̃ᵢ = 1 for the single best member, 0 otherwise

It sits permanently at the degeneracy the real PF only falls into occasionally. It is best-member selection, not Bayesian inference, and it is kept as a cheap reference rather than a competitor. The "Selection" column in Results is this scheme; the "PF (OpenDA)" column is the real SIR filter.

docs.title: Perturbation calibration
docs.text:
Each member gets one AR(1) noise series per variable added to the control Forcing.dat:

xₜ = φ·xₜ₋₁ + σ·εₜ ,      ε ~ N(0,1) ,      φ = exp(−1/τ)

The two parameters are fitted from different data and kept strictly separate.

Amplitude: measured. The stationary standard deviation σ/√(1−φ²) is fitted from the ICON residual, s = std(ICON lake mean − control Forcing.dat): how far the reanalysis actually strays from the control forcing. Fitted once per lake and committed. This stands for a realistic representativeness error of the original station forcing.

Persistence: bracketed, not measured. No dataset gives us the decorrelation time of the forcing forecast error, so we bracket it between two proxies, each biased in a known direction:

  • Floor: the ACF of the ICON residual. An approximation of the error ACF after averaging; its 1/e crossing comes early.
  • Ceiling: the ACF of the station signal itself. This measures how long the weather persists, not how long the error does. A forecast already captures the slow synoptic structure and fails on the fast small-scale part, so the error is enriched in fast components and should decorrelate sooner.

On Upper Lugano GLOB that gives 1.39 h < τ_err < 7.17 h.

The envelope is the production choice: per channel, take whichever end has the longer τ. Two reasons. First, the bracket does not always hold: on Maggiore V, Geneva V and Hallwil U the supposed floor e-folds later than the ceiling, which falsifies the floor argument on those channels, because that residual is carrying a slowly drifting bias rather than white grid noise. Second, and decisively, taking the shorter end would shorten persistence, and short persistence costs spread. Under-dispersion is the failure mode we already have and want to avoid.

Two traps this encoding avoids.

Never fit AR(1) to raw GLOB. Its autocorrelation is dominated by the diurnal cycle, not by cloud persistence: a lag-1 correlation of 0.934 implies τ = 14.67 h, while the ACF actually e-folds at 4.28 h. The ACF is periodic, not exponential, so fitting it raw injects a radiation too persistent perturbation. GLOB is fitted on the clearness index (GLOB / clear-sky, daytime only); wind on the diurnal anomaly, with the lake breeze effect removed.

σ is not the perturbation's size: it is the size of one hourly kick. The spread is σ/√(1−φ²), because a persistent process accumulates its past kicks. Raising φ at fixed σ therefore also raises the amplitude, which confounds persistence with amplitude and makes the comparison uninterpretable. So σ is always re-derived to hold the stationary std at the ICON-fitted value, σ = s·√(1−φ²). Note that σ falls as the perturbation becomes more persistent: smaller kicks, but they accumulate further.

Both bounds are stored with the lake's perturbation (operational-simstrat static/assimilation/<lake>.json, perturbations.persistence; perturbations/<lake>.json at 20564a9); stationary_std is stored once and both bounds derive their σ from it, so the two ends cannot drift apart in amplitude.

docs.title: Open problems
docs.text:
Last updated: November 2026.

In short

The observation side is in good shape; the open problems are on the model side. The main one is that the ensemble is too narrow, especially at depth. Most of the other problems below follow from it.

docs.title: 1. The ensemble is too narrow
docs.text:
The problems we tried to solve with the observation uncertainty all point to an under-dispersed ensemble. In every calibration σ occupies almost the entire uncertainty budget, because the spread has little to contribute at depth (Results). The single biggest limitation of the current setup: spread is generated only at the surface, through three forcing variables, and reaches depth only by mixing.

What we know. Parameter perturbation adds spread in the right place but only at amplitudes that cannot be justified (Parameter perturbation). Perturbing air temperature adds nothing, particularly in winter where we were hoping to see an effect on the mixing structure (Geneva CTD).

First answer: a learned model error. A process noise q on the temperature profile, learned online together with the observation error R, makes the spread follow the error: spread/RMSE 0.26 → 0.98 on Upper Lugano and 0.22 → 0.76 on Ägeri (against the filtered observations), with slightly lower RMSE on both (−5 % and −8 % against the raw observations) (Learned R and q, Ägeri check).

Suggested next steps. Port it to master and test it on the other lakes; 7-day reforecasts to see whether the band holds at longer leads; the deep water in summer, where q drops to 0 and the band is still too narrow. Parameter spread at lower assimilation frequency remains an option.

docs.title: 2. The forcing ensemble is not centred
docs.text:
The perturbation noise on the wind components U and V has zero mean, but the wind speed does not: every member is windier than the control. In the later CTD runs the ensemble-mean wind speed was 31–63 % above the control's (Centred forcing perturbations), and the operational setup (simplified_final) uses the same uncentred perturbation. The ensemble mean therefore carries a systematic extra mixing that the daily analysis has to correct every day, and that accumulates when the observations are far apart.

Suggested next step. Rerun simplified_final with center_perturbations and compare RMSE, spread and NIS with the current results; repeat the Lugano deep-mixing run with centred forcing.

docs.title: 3. The summer thermocline
docs.text:
Most places where the analysis is worse than the free run sit at the thermocline in summer (Results). The error there is structural: the model misplaces the thermocline, and a forcing-generated ensemble rarely contains the right profile. Every σ variant we tried either left it unchanged or made it worse (Experiments).

The learned model error helps here first: on Ägeri the 12–14 m error drops from 0.45–0.60 °C with simplified_final, which at 12–12.4 m is even slightly worse than the free run, to 0.38–0.51 °C, below the free run at every level (Ägeri check). The price is larger corrections at the thermocline (up to 1.4 °C on Ägeri and 2.0 °C on Upper Lugano).

Suggested next steps. Check whether the large corrections at the thermocline are physical or shocks (the day after each), and whether a step cap is needed; parameter spread at lower assimilation frequency.

docs.title: 4. The filter is over-cautious
docs.text:
With the seasonal σ the filter is systematically too cautious (NIS ≈ 0.6): it says it is less sure than it really is, and deep observations are trusted far too little. Calibrating σ fixes the consistency but not the accuracy (Experiments).

Suggested next step. Revisit σ once the ensemble carries more spread; σ should then not have to fill the whole budget!

This is now possible: with the learned R and q the model error is carried by the ensemble, and R takes only the misses that do not repeat from day to day. Without q (R split only) R stays physical and there is no runaway as with adaptive σ, but the filter swings to over-confident (NIS 1.76 on Ägeri). With q it is close to consistent (NIS 1.29 on Upper Lugano, 0.67 on Ägeri). Open: why Ägeri ends on the cautious side.

docs.title: 5. Lakes with surface data only
docs.text:
Several lakes have only a surface station. Surface-only assimilation corrects the surface but damages the layers just below, between about 10 and 35 m against CTD (Surface-only). Nothing we tried on the observation side fixed it.

Suggested next step. Localization limited to the mixed layer, so that surface information is not pushed below it; or, where possible, at least a few sensors over the upper 30–40 m (assimilating deeper sensor 15 m together or CTD).

docs.title: 6. Deep mixing
docs.text:
Assimilating long-term CTD casts corrects the deep temperatures but makes deep mixing more frequent, 15 winters instead of 10 on Lake Lugano (Deep mixing).

Part of this may come from the uncentred forcing ensemble (problem 2).

docs.title: 7. Ensemble size and evaluation period
docs.text:
Twenty members is what the operational chain can afford, not a statistically defended choice. And every result is scored on 2025, the only year with profile observations on all seven lakes; the fitting-year check covers only three lakes (Fitting year).

Suggested next step. Score each new year as it becomes available, with the σ fitted on the previous ones. The learned R and q need no fitted σ; only the depth correlation of q comes from one year, and pooling more years would make it a lake property.

docs.title: 8. Physically defensible parameters
docs.text:
Estimating parameters with the filter does not converge: the parameters follow the seasons and absorb the model's seasonal bias (Joint estimation).

Suggested next step. Slower updates; and compare the estimated distribution with a traditional calibration and learn model weaknesses.

docs.title: 9. 3D: horizontal spurious correlations
docs.text:
In 3D one buoy can correct a whole region, but with 7 members spurious horizontal correlations are a real concern, and the first runs point to the need for vertical localization (3D).

Suggested next step. Vertical and horizontal localization; assimilating the satellite surface temperature using scaling to adapt the vertical resolution.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Last updated: November 2026. All results are for the 2025 calendar year unless stated otherwise.

In short

An ensemble Kalman filter corrects the Alplakes Simstrat models with in-situ temperature profiles. On seven lakes the operational setup lowers the hourly error by 25–50 %, at every depth on five of them. Most of the work went into the observation side; what is left is a model-spread problem: the ensemble is too narrow, especially at depth in the current setup. We propose possible fixes, which need further testing and possibly more work (Open problems).

Alplakes runs one-dimensional Simstrat simulations for many lakes in the alpine region. The models are calibrated, and they can still be significantly wrong from time to time (errors of up to 2 °C, sustained for weeks, are common). Meanwhile, moored thermistor chains and profilers sit in several of those same lakes reporting temperature every few minutes/hours.

Data assimilation is the right machinery for putting those two things in the same product. This workblog documents the module we built for it, in collaboration with the Canton of Ticino: the filters, the choices behind them, results across seven lakes, and, with equal weight, the things that still could need further work.

A large share of the effort described here went into making the filter more fair, and it did not make it more accurate.

docs.text:
Figure 1. Alplakes performance panel, Castagnola buoy, Lake Lugano, 0.5 m, end of August 2026: measurement (red), Delft3D-FLOW, Simstrat and the assimilated Simstrat run (BETA).

Figure 1 is the Alplakes performance panel for the Castagnola buoy on Lake Lugano at 0.5 m depth, data from Canton Ticino at the end of August 2026. The red line is the measurement. In summer both models sit well off it: Delft3D-FLOW about 1.8 °C, and Simstrat, the 1D model under focus here, also about 1.8 °C. The assimilated Simstrat run, sharing the same calibrated 1D model with the filter switched on, is at 0.41 °C error.

That panel is the BETA for Upper Lugano, and it is roughly what the finished product should look like. We extended (and calibrated) the EnKF filter to six further lakes with high-frequency in-situ data: Ägeri, Greifensee, Murten, Maggiore, Geneva and Hallwil.

docs.title: What the module provides
docs.text:
Any ensemble filter needs four ingredients:

  • An ensemble: N perturbed copies of the model run in parallel, each with its own restart file. The spread between members is the model's uncertainty.
  • Observations: measured values at known times, with a stated uncertainty that tells the filter how much to trust them.
  • A state vector: what gets corrected at each update. For the 1D model in our experiments the temperature profile.
  • An update cycle: the model runs until an observation arrives, the filter computes a correction for each member (or samples among the members), the corrected state is written back into the restart, and the model carries on until the next observation.

In practice that means we need a calibrated model, a real-time in-situ data source, an ensemble mechanism, and a filter. The module provides the last two:

  1. A forcing-perturbation mechanism, which is how the ensemble is generated (Method).
  2. Two interchangeable engines: a customisable Python implementation and a parallel OpenDA setup, running a simple selection of the best-fitting member (Python), a particle filter (OpenDA), an Ensemble Kalman Filter (Python and OpenDA), and further versions thereof (OpenDA) (Method).

It is currently designed for lakes with high-resolution in-situ profiles at sub-daily frequency.

docs.title: Headline numbers
docs.text:
• −25 to −50 % hourly RMSE on all seven lakes, pooled over depths and the year (Results).
  • Every model level improves on five of seven lakes.
  • The EnKF beats best-member selection and the particle filter on every lake; selection is worse than no assimilation on three (Results).
  • Native and OpenDA EnKF agree within 0.01–0.04 °C, which validates the custom implementation.
  • 🔬 Preliminary, two lakes: learning the observation and model errors online is a possible fix for the narrow ensemble. First tests are slightly more accurate (−5 to −8 % RMSE) but need further testing (Learning the errors online).

docs.title: What we can say so far
docs.text:
A fixed seasonal σ is ready and is a good operational solution: 25 % or more improvement across seven lakes with high-resolution profiles, up to ~50 % in the best case.

Forcing perturbations keep corrections small, so the model is never shocked. That makes the scheme safe to run unattended.

The large observation error also counteracts the over-confidence that correlated, closely spaced observations would otherwise possibly generate.

Near-surface seasonal bias is corrected reliably: one of the major free-run failures.

Profile data and seiche filtering each improve and allow improvements at intermediate depths in summer; filtered profile data is central to a filter that works over the whole water column.

Surface assimilation improves the upper layers, but it cannot satisfactorily correct the whole profile in a 1D model; against low-resolution CTD data we show evidence that it can significantly damage the layers just below.

Calibrating is useful for consistency, not so much for accuracy: optimising calibration across seven lakes changed the RMSE by little overall. Estimating σ on the fly made every lake consistent but could run away (Ägeri): it blamed every miss on the observations. Learning the observation and model errors separately avoids this in first tests on two lakes, but needs further testing (preliminary, Learning the errors online).

The work described here is almost entirely on the observation side. What is left is a model-spread problem; a learned model error q is one possible answer (Open problems).

When does the filter perform best? It performs best in the stratified season, and mostly inside the mixed layer. The gain front follows the mixed layer down through autumn (Results), because the spread is made at the surface by wind and radiation and can only reach depth by mixing. So the filter is most useful exactly where the model has a seasonal surface-energy bias; less useful in winter, because the model errors are smaller; and worst at the summer thermocline, because that error is structural and difficult to overcome completely. The next real gain may come more from the model side and the accurate description of its structural uncertainties, rather than from the observations (Open problems).

docs.title: Run configuration behind the numbers
docs.text:
The operational setup is called simplified_final. The numbers on these pages were made with the code at commit 20564a9, where its σ values are in args/run_enkf.json.

  • Ensemble: 20 members, generated by AR(1) forcing perturbation on wind U, wind V and solar radiation.
  • Period: 2025 calendar year, daily assimilation at a per-lake night-time hour (23Z–06Z).
  • Engines: native Python EnKF and OpenDA, configured from identical inputs, perturbed forcings, warmup and observation series, so that residual differences are the algorithm alone.
  • Observations: causally filtered below 4 m with a per-lake seiche-derived window, thinned to a per-lake target vertical grid, retained at the assimilation hour.
  • Observation error: fixed per lake and season (mixed / stratified, stratified = May to October); Ägeri one value for the whole year.
  • Scoring: RMSE and CRPS against the raw observations (unfiltered, averaged into hourly bins centred on the full hour), at every observed depth within the model, over the hours all compared runs share. Consistency measures (band coverage, spread/RMSE) against the filtered observations at the assimilated depths, the series the observation error describes, with the raw value in brackets where both are given. NIS is computed by the filter at each analysis, against the observations it assimilates. The surface-only comparison and the CTD check of adaptive σ are scored against CTD casts.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Free run The model run without assimilation, from the same start; the baseline every gain is measured against. Analysis The state after the filter has corrected it with an observation. Ensemble, member The N perturbed copies of the model run in parallel; one copy is a member. Spread The standard deviation across the members: the model's own uncertainty. Innovation Observation minus model forecast at the observed depth, before the correction. Increment, correction How much the analysis changes the state. σ (observation error) The uncertainty handed to the filter for each observation. Here a representativeness error, not instrument error. Representativeness error What the model cannot reproduce: variability a 1D column cannot produce (e.g. internal waves) and the difference between a point measurement and a lake-wide column. Uncertainty budget The total uncertainty the filter expects, √(spread² + σ²), against the actual model–observation gap. NIS Normalised innovation squared, d² / (spread² + σ²). 1 = consistent, below 1 over-cautious, above 1 over-confident. Calibration (of the filter) How close NIS is to 1. Not the same as accuracy. Mixed / stratified season November–April / May–October. Seiche filtering Causal trailing average below 4 m, over one internal-seiche period, removing thermocline displacement the 1D model cannot reproduce. Localization Forcing small, probably spurious correlations between distant depths to zero in the update. Under-dispersion The ensemble spread is smaller than the actual error. Native / OpenDA engine The project's own Python implementation, and the setup running the same filter through OpenDA.

docs.title: FAQ
docs.text:
Why only 20 members? Cost, in the operational chain. Twenty is what we can afford daily across seven lakes. It is a real limitation, not a choice we would defend on statistical grounds.

Isn't filtering the observations just throwing away real signal? Yes, and deliberately. The sensor is right and the signal is real. But it is an internal-wave displacement that a 1D column cannot produce, so feeding it to the filter asks the model to reproduce something it structurally cannot.

Why does better calibration not give better accuracy? Calibration means the filter's stated uncertainty matches the innovations it sees. That is self-consistency. It says nothing about whether the correction goes in the right direction at the right depth.

What is the single biggest limitation? Ensemble under-dispersion. We generate spread only at the surface, through three forcing variables, and it reaches depth only by mixing (Open problems).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Last updated: October 2026. Operational setup (simplified_final), 2025, 20 members; scored against hourly observations unless stated otherwise. Full run configuration in Reference.

In short

The EnKF wins on every lake, on both engines, and lowers the hourly RMSE by 26–51 %. The error peak at the thermocline or surface is lowered, not moved. The gain follows the mixed layer down through the year, because that is where the ensemble has spread. The filter is mostly over-cautious: σ fills almost the whole uncertainty budget, and the corrections are small.

docs.text:

The EnKF wins on every lake, on both engines, and not marginally.

Best-member selection is worse than not assimilating at all on three of seven lakes: Greifensee (1.67 vs 1.09), Ägeri (0.84 vs 0.46), Murten (0.95 vs 0.72). If no member has the right profile, selecting one cannot help, and collapsing the choice to a single member appears to be worse than resampling more often than not. The two Ticino lakes are the exceptions where both selection and PF help.

The native and OpenDA EnKF agree to within 0.01–0.04 °C on every lake. The two configurations are built from identical inputs, identical perturbed forcings, identical warmup and identical observation series. The agreement validates our custom implementation.

In the top 10 m the PF and selection perform much closer to the EnKF: near the surface the perturbation acts directly, so the ensemble develops genuine spread and picking the best member can pick a modified enough profile. At depth the members are very close to each other, there is nothing to choose between, and the member selected for its surface fit arrives carrying its own deep profile. The PF's failure is a deep-profile failure, and it is the concrete cost of not building a per-depth correction.

Pooled hourly over the year, for each depth, RMSE in °C (Figure 2):

Figure 2. RMSE against depth, free run (grey) vs analysis (colour), all seven lakes, 2025; green fill is the gain.

Free run in grey, analysis in colour, green fill is the gain.

Every lake improves by at least 25%. On five of seven lakes every single model level improves. The exceptions are Greifensee (around 7 m and between 11 and 13.5 m) and, more mildly, Ägeri (between 11 and 13 m). Every lake's error peaks at the thermocline or at the surface, and the analysis lowers that peak without moving it. The filter does not relocate the difficulty. Gains are often largest at the surface, and on some lakes the two curves converge in the deeper layers. Geneva's and Hallwil's spikes are data gaps.

docs.title: In time and depth
docs.text:
Figure 3. RMSE change against the free run by depth and month, all seven lakes, 2025.

The same gain resolved by month (Figure 3). On Upper Lugano, Maggiore, Hallwil and Murten a green staircase descends with depth through the year, following the seasonal stratification.

The filter can only correct effectively where it has covariance, a model-observation gap, and where ensemble spread exists. Our spread is created at the surface, by wind and radiation, and reaches depth only by mixing. So the staircase traces the depth to which the ensemble is still dispersed effectively and where significant model error is present.

In winter the model errors are smaller, so corrections and gains are smaller too, and the panels fade toward white. Most of the significant red patches, where the analysis is worse than the free run, group around the thermocline in summer: it remains the challenging region.

docs.title: Is the filter honest?
docs.text: Accuracy is one question. Whether the filter's stated uncertainty matches the errors it actually sees is a different one.

docs.title: The uncertainty budget
docs.text:
Figure 4. Uncertainty budget by depth, all seven lakes, 2025: ensemble spread, observation error σ, model–observation gap and pooled target.

In Figure 4, blue is ensemble spread, green the assumed observation error, black the model–observation gap, orange the pooled target √(spread² + σ²), which is what the filter expects the gap to be.

The observation error occupies essentially the whole uncertainty budget, and the spread collapses to near zero at depth for certain lakes, a direct consequence of perturbing only surface forcing. This balance is what actually governs how large the corrections can be.

The model–observation gap (black) falls with depth on every lake, after a local maximum at intermediate depths. Where black and orange disagree the filter is not self-consistent: where black crosses above orange it is over-confident, where it sits below it is damped. Ägeri and Hallwil appear again as outlier cases. Overall, the setup tends to be over-cautious.

docs.title: In time and depth
docs.text:
Figure 5. Normalised innovation squared (NIS) by depth and month, all seven lakes, 2025.

The same comparison resolved in time (Figure 5), as the normalised innovation squared (NIS), d² / (spread² + σ²): green is consistent, blue over-damped, red over-confident. The map is mostly blue: the filter is systematically too cautious and assumes more error than it actually sees. Observations in the deep column are particularly affected by the fixed-profile approximation and are trusted far too little. Where the filter is over-confident is spring, during the large model biases, and then sporadically in the deeper layers. Ägeri, with a very polarised profile in depth, and Hallwil are the odd cases.

docs.title: What the corrections look like
docs.text:
Figure 6 shows the absolute EnKF correction per analysis against depth for each lake, on a log scale: thick bars mark the typical range (interquartile range), thin lines the full range, dots the median at the observed depths, and the box gives the median and the largest single correction.

Figure 6. Absolute EnKF correction per analysis by depth, all seven lakes, 2025, log scale.

Because the spread is narrow and the observation error large in proportion, corrections are steered toward the observations only weakly: median increments over column and time are 0.006–0.027 °C, typically much smaller than the spread or the gap. The large increments (up to 0.3–1.4 °C) come from large innovations, and those live at the surface and, above all, where the model's thermocline and the observed one disagree. Below the stratification the correction magnitude decays down to a flat minimum, a structure that probably reflects the mixing activity in each lake.
